This finding extends and refines a previous result by Polster regarding the automorphism group of the moduli space of stable bundles on the Hirzebruch surface of degree 2.

Retinal surgeons face a significant challenge in navigating the complex, curved surface of the retina, particularly when operating on delicate structures. To overcome this obstacle, a novel 3D guidance system is introduced, utilizing the spotlight projection method to enhance depth perception. This innovative approach leverages the spotlight mechanism to create a localized, high-resolution 3D image of the retina, allowing for more precise control. To evaluate its effectiveness, a phantom dataset was created, simulating real-world conditions, and the proposed method was compared to a state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction technique. The results demonstrate that the spotlight projection method achieves comparable accuracy while significantly reducing computational requirements, thus facilitating its use in real-time surgical settings. The proposed method also offers a unique, intuitive 3D visualization of the retina, enabling surgeons to make more informed decisions.

The $F$-polynomials, which are defined as the weighted sums of the $\hat{F}$-polynomials, can be expressed as a sum with alternating signs and coefficients that depend on the weights and the variable $x$. This formula has a straightforward proof and can be used to derive various properties, including the fact that the roots of the $F$-polynomials change sign and can be expressed as a difference of two sets of $\hat{F}$-roots. Additionally, the formula can be utilized to establish the relationship between the Newton polytopes of $\hat{F}$-polynomials when the weights are distinct.

The FIDO2 initiative, a collaborative project between Google, Microsoft, and others, has been instrumental in driving the shift away from password-based authentication towards more secure, passwordless authentication methods. This transition is being spearheaded by FIDO2's adoption by major tech companies, including Apple, Amazon, and Microsoft, and its integration into their respective platforms. Notably, FIDO2's support for Web authentication allows users to leverage their security credentials, such as U2F keys, and utilize them seamlessly in web browsers, and this technology has been successfully implemented by prominent companies like YubiKey, Teslacrypt, and YOLO.

A novel Weyl-Wigner formalism has been developed for non-commutative spaces, which are defined by a central extension of a group. This formalism is applied to the Heisenberg group to study quantum systems within two-dimensional complex space. However, the resulting quantum mechanics lacks precision when dealing with qubit-specific phenomena, and its application to the group $SU(2)$ through a complex sphere yields inconsistent results for the Hamiltonian operator.

The widespread use of video apps has become a standard part of daily life, with users of all ages accessing a vast array of content through these apps. Despite their ubiquity, however, the design of these apps often fails to account for the diverse needs and preferences of their users, who may require more control over their experience. This study explores the ways in which users interact with video apps, with a focus on how users can be given greater control through the incorporation of new user interface elements. Twenty users participated in a study that involved watching a video and then completing a follow-up survey, with the results indicating that users often struggle to find the necessary tools for managing their experience. This has led to the identification of several key design principles that could be used to improve the design of video apps and enhance the sense of control offered to their users.

We introduce a new class of Turing machines known as reactive, called rTMs, which can simulate the behaviour of standard Turing machines but with one key difference. rTMs can also produce output continuously as they run, much like the π-calculus. We demonstrate that this continuous output capability makes rTMs capable of modelling systems that cannot be replicated using traditional, finitely executable systems. Interestingly, this continuous output capability is not unique to rTMs; the π-calculus also possesses this characteristic. We establish a connection between the π-calculus and rTMs by showing that both can be used to model the same types of systems and that there is a one-to-one relationship between the two, with some minor adjustments.

A new binary Gray code for ordered trees has been developed, which enables the step-by-step transformation between any two trees without going through an intermediate tree. This new code builds on a previous order-invariant Gray code for plane trees and has been expanded to cover all binary trees. The novel Gray code has been achieved by employing a modified approach to the method used in plane tree Gray codes and by overcoming the challenges associated with ordered trees that have multiple children. The new code has been successfully implemented in the HOIST system and has been used to compute the Betti numbers of ordered trees with up to 9 vertices.

The track reconstruction process in heavy ion collision events is complicated by the presence of numerous interactions between particles, resulting in high densities of secondary vertices and significant amounts of secondary interactions between particles. This results in a high rate of fake tracks, which must be removed by the algorithm. The algorithm used to achieve this is described in detail, along with the results of efficiency calculations and the effects of various algorithm parameters. The algorithm's performance is evaluated using simulated data and compared to actual data collected by the ALICE detector at the LHC.

A novel numerical method called the Discontinuous Prismatic Space-Time (D-PST) approach has been developed to simulate fluid flow on a free surface. This method utilizes a continuous space-time formulation, where prismatic elements are employed to model the flow domain. By doing so, it mitigates the challenges associated with discontinuous finite-elements, such as the formation of spurious oscillations. The proposed method incorporates a second-order central difference scheme for the space-time domain, ensuring the satisfaction of the mass conservation principle. The method's performance has been successfully validated through a series of benchmark tests, including the dam break problem and a test case involving a solitary wave crashing onto a submerged wall.

Given a signed graph, we investigate the existence of a circular $r_k$-flow, where $r_k$ represents the set of all vertices with odd in-degrees modulo $k$. We derive conditions for the flow's existence in signed graphs and demonstrate its relationship to the concept of $\mathcal{O}_{k}^{+}(G)$. Our findings are further generalized to $k$-edge-regular signed graphs. Additionally, we explore the computational complexity of the problem and its connection to the $\mathcal{O}_{k}^{+}(G)$ problem.

We present a straightforward, deterministic algorithm for the Modular Subset Sum problem, which is the problem of finding all non-empty subsets of a given set whose sum is divisible by a specified positive integer $m$. Our algorithm can be efficiently parallelized and runs in $O(nm)$ time and $O(n)$ space, provided that the input set contains $n$ elements. This is the first algorithm that is fully deterministic to solve this problem within the same level of time complexity as its randomized counterpart, which is known to have an optimal time bound of $\Theta(nm)$.

We have compiled a list of 20 M dwarf stars that exhibit rotational variability and flare events, with observations taken from the Kepler mission, the TESS mission, and ground-based telescopes. Our research identified 15 stars that displayed flare events, with 10 of them also showing rotational variability. Our observations of flare events align with previous findings on M dwarfs, with some stars experiencing multiple flares in a single observation. We discovered that flare events occur more frequently in stars with higher effective temperatures, with a notable exception of one star that exhibited a flare event despite having the lowest effective temperature in our sample. Our research also revealed that flare events are more common in stars that exhibit rotational variability, with a notable difference in the distribution of periods of these stars. Our findings suggest that flare events are more common in stars that exhibit rotational variability, with a notable difference in the distribution of periods of these stars.

The amplatoid larvae of the red-eyed green dragonfly undergo a dramatic transformation in their immune response, exhibiting distinct crawling patterns that are absent in earlier stages. Researchers have found that the absence of certain immune cells called hemocytes is crucial for normal crawling behavior in these dragonfly larvae. To understand this phenomenon, scientists studied the movement of these cells in different genetic contexts and found that the absence of these cells is associated with abnormal crawling patterns. Specifically, overexpression of certain genes led to increased cellular adhesion and resulted in abnormal crawling behavior. These results suggest that the absence of these cells is essential for normal crawling behavior in these dragonfly larvae, and that the role of these cells is to regulate the movement of these cells in a context-dependent manner.

We introduce c-siam, a cutting-edge architecture for speech-text alignment that
utilizes convolutional neural networks to extract both low and high-level audio
features. This approach enables the model to capture a broader range of linguistic
information, spanning from phonemes to sentences. c-siam's robust feature
extraction capabilities, combined with its ability to learn from diverse data
sources, allows it to achieve superior performance on a range of benchmark tests
compared to existing methods.

A revised version of the B\"uttiker--B\"uhr--Harms model accurately predicts the total cross sections of neutrino interactions with nucleons and nuclei, aligning closely with experimental measurements and the predictions of the MiniBooNE and T2K experiments. This updated model also yields consistent results for differential cross sections and selection ratios, thereby confirming its validity.

This research explores the almost certain stabilization of an adaptive control system whose state is represented by a hidden Markov process. The approach relies on a state observer that can accurately estimate the system's state based on output data. The analysis demonstrates that the system's state and output estimates converge to their actual values over time. Building upon this, it is shown that the system's output can be used to derive an adaptive stabilizing controller. The almost certain stability of this controller is proven using Lyapunov functions and a compactness argument. The research also presents a simulation to support its findings.

This paper introduces a novel approach to task assignment and invocation in distributed systems, known as BTAI. Building on the principles of its predecessors, BIPAI and PBAI, which employed a hierarchical tree-based model for task assignment and invocation, BTAI incorporates a more efficient and adaptive framework that optimizes task completion by selecting the most suitable processing node or invocation method. A comprehensive performance evaluation of BTAI was conducted using a benchmark test suite, which assessed its efficacy in diverse task types and complex execution graphs. The results indicate that BTAI surpasses its predecessors in task completion speed and efficiency, yielding notable improvements of 8.6%, 12.5%, and 16.4% over BIPAI, PBAI, and the average performance of the three approaches, respectively.

The equation of state for the quark gluon plasma is used to derive the Korteveg-de Vries equation in relativistic heavy ion collisions. This equation is numerically solved to obtain the scaling solution, which is then compared to experimental data from pion transverse momentum spectra. The scaling solution is used to analyze the formation of the quark gluon plasma in ultra-relativistic heavy ion collisions.

The space of continuous real-valued functions on a compact space is linearly Eberlein-Grothendieck precisely when it can be represented as a closed subset of $C(K)\), where $K$ is a compact subset of $\ell_2$-space. Consequently, the Eberlein-Gothe space $E(G)$ associated with any topological group $G$ is linearly Eberlein-Grothendieck if and only if $G$ is homeomorphic to a subset of $\ell_2$.

We provide a direct link between the second quantized form of a Hamiltonian and its Taylor coefficients as a function of phase space. This connection is used to illustrate that a Hamiltonian with constant frequency for a particular invariant manifold can still be non-isochronic. Furthermore, we introduce a new definition of isochronicity based on the second quantized form, showing that a system is isochronic if and only if the Hamiltonian's second quantized form has constant frequency for all invariant manifolds.

The Lorenz system is a 3-dimensional autonomous model that exhibits periodic, quasi-periodic, and chaotic behaviors. In this study, we employed the harmonic analysis method to identify and classify various periodic orbits of the Lorenz system with distinct period lengths. Periodic orbits with period 1 through 7 were cataloged based on their stability and bifurcation patterns. Period-1 solutions were found to be stable and can be obtained from a stable equilibrium point or a limit cycle in the Rossler system. Period-2 solutions were identified as a pair of limit cycles in the Lorenz system, emerging from the system's equilibrium points. Period-3 solutions were found to be a triple loop structure consisting of two limit cycles and a saddle point in the Lorenz system, resulting from a period-2 solution in the Rossler system. Period-4, period-5, and period-7 solutions were discovered in the Lorenz system, representing a quadruple loop, a double double loop, and a double double double loop structures, respectively. The study also revealed that period-7 solutions in the Lorenz system can be obtained from period-3 solutions in the Rossler system. The research showed that the harmonic analysis method is effective in identifying periodic orbits in the Lorenz system and Rossler system, and their counterparts in other systems.

This research delves into the stochastic differential calculus on statistical manifolds, specifically focusing on the stochastic Malliavin calculus and its application to parameter estimation in statistical models. We demonstrate that the Malliavin calculus yields derivatives of the log-likelihood function, which can be viewed as the right-hand side of the score equation. This connection enables us to explore the Malliavin rank of parameter estimates and establish a relationship with the geometric properties of the statistical manifold. Furthermore, we establish that the Malliavin rank is bounded by the Frobenius rank, with equality achievable under standard assumptions.

We investigate the behavior of critical exponents for representations of the fundamental group of a closed surface that undergo deformation via Teichmüller flow. Our findings demonstrate that the spectrum of the Laplacian at singularities dictates the dependence on the Teichmüller deformation. This discovery enables us to determine the asymptotic behavior of the maximal Lyapunov exponent in various scenarios.

We introduce an autoregressive extension to the Fourier transform, which enables the representation of time-series data in a more meaningful way. This enhancement allows for the removal of noise from time-series data, which in turn improves model performance on prediction models. We validate the effectiveness of our approach by demonstrating its benefits in enhancing the performance of state-of-the-art models on multiple time-series datasets.

We have conducted a comprehensive examination of the compatibility of the cosmological model with various observational datasets, specifically focusing on the relationship between cosmic density parameters and the equation of state within a spatially flat universe framework. Our analysis is based on the assumption that the universe is in a state of dynamic equilibrium, and we have used multiple datasets, including supernovae type Ia observations, baryon acoustic oscillation measurements, and Hubble parameter data, to constrain the parameters of the cosmological density parameters and the equation of state. Our findings indicate that the datasets are highly consistent, and we have found that the parameters of the cosmic density parameters and the equation of state are within the following ranges: $\Omega_{\rm m} \in [0.5, 0.7]$, $\Omega_{\rm de} \in [0.73, 0.85]$, and $w \in [-1.1, -0.9]$. Our results also suggest that the universe is undergoing accelerated expansion, and we have found that the Hubble parameter is consistent with the values obtained from the Planck satellite.

This paper addresses the challenge of optimizing resource allocation for service function chaining in multi-access edge computing environments, breaking down the complex problem into two smaller components: selecting the most effective service function chain mapping and determining the corresponding network flow. To achieve this, we developed a novel algorithm that iteratively refines the mapping solution through a series of network flow calculations, while also ensuring that the associated edge servers can handle the necessary processing loads. To address the associated computational complexity, we created a more efficient flow-based algorithm that utilizes a tailored mapping search strategy and a more effective flow-based solution that leverages a modified version of the network flow algorithm. Our results demonstrate that these algorithms significantly outperform existing methods in terms of resource utilization and service quality.

We investigate the impact of disorder on the topological phase transitions in a two-dimensional model of Dirac fermions with a Zeeman spin-splitting. The model is based on a square lattice with a nearest-neighbor hopping Hamiltonian and is subjected to a uniform magnetic field. The system's behavior is analyzed through the topological charge of the Chern number, which indicates the presence of either a quantum Hall insulator with a Chern number of 0 or a topological insulator with a Chern number of 2. The results show that the system undergoes a quantum phase transition from a topological insulator to a quantum Hall insulator as the Zeeman spin-splitting increases. The transition is influenced by the strength of the disorder, which causes the transition point to shift and the topological phase to become less stable. The system's behavior is characterized by the mean-field theory, which accurately predicts the transition point and the topological properties of the system. The results are also supported by numerical simulations using the density matrix renormalization group method.

This study examines the impact of positive experiences on users with depression. We compare the effects of positive events on users with depression to those without and explore the factors that contribute to these differences. Our analysis of Twitter data reveals that users with depression report more positive events, such as celebrations of loved ones' birthdays and significant work achievements, than those without the condition. However, these positive events are less likely to be shared by users with depression, suggesting a potential disparity in users' social support and the visibility of their positive experiences.

A QCD-based theory with an additional dark matter component could provide insight into dark matter's composition and behavior. The presence of a baryon asymmetry in such a theory might be achieved through a process involving baryon number violation and the decay of heavy quarks into lighter ones. The resulting baryon asymmetry could be substantial, potentially exceeding that in our observable universe by a factor of ten thousand. The resulting universe would be characterized by a unique temperature and chemical composition, featuring a dark matter component that is strongly interacting and relatively cold. The quark-based universe would be hotter and more dense near the core, where the quark-gluon plasma would be in thermal equilibrium with the dark matter component.

A new compound, Na$_{4-\delta}$NiTeO$_6$, is discovered and its magnetic properties are examined through the combination of neutron powder diffraction and muon spin relaxation. The results reveal that the Ni$^{2+}$ spin in the compound has a notably smaller size, approximately 1.2 $\mu_B$ at 1.8 K, which is significantly reduced due to the crystalline electric field effect. The compound exhibits a complex magnetic structure at low temperatures, featuring a spin glass-like behavior. The muon spin relaxation data indicate the presence of a spin glass glass state at low temperatures, characterized by a slow spin relaxation and a long-range spin correlation. The compound's magnetic properties are further explored through the application of a magnetic field, which leads to the formation of a spin glass state. The compound's magnetic behavior is also influenced by the presence of a crystal field effect, resulting in a unique spin glass-like state.

As the Internet of Things (IoT) continues to grow, large-scale distributed systems will rely heavily on automated decision-making, which in turn will depend on trust levels within these systems.  However, the IoT's vast and unpredictable nature makes traditional trust management systems ineffective, prompting the need for a new approach.  This research aims to address this challenge by developing a dynamic trust and reputation model that leverages Bayesian Network (BN) technology.  BNs are particularly well-suited for modeling complex IoT scenarios, but their integration with trust and reputation in this context is a novel application.  This study proposes a new framework that combines BNs with Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) to create a continuous learning and updating mechanism for trust and reputation.  It also introduces a new metric for quantifying trust and reputation, which is then evaluated using a simulation-based approach.

In various fields, cubic splines are widely employed due to their ability to approximate data with a smooth curve. However, the preservation of data monotonicity is crucial in certain applications, such as finance, where the requirement for monotonicity is often necessary. This paper introduces a novel approach to monotone cubic splines, leveraging the properties of subdifferentials to derive necessary monotonicity constraints from the original spline formulation. The resulting method is straightforward to implement and offers a computationally efficient solution to monotone spline approximation.

This study explores the characteristics of a type of exact black bounce solution within both de Sitter and anti-de Sitter frameworks. We discovered that the solution's behavior is influenced by the choice of metric function, and that the solution can be affected by a phase transition triggered by a change in the metric. Notably, the solution exhibits distinct features in de Sitter and anti-de Sitter frameworks, and that the solution can be scaled to represent different black hole states. We also found that the solution's energy conditions are consistent with the null energy condition, and that the solution's thermodynamic properties can be analyzed using the first law of thermodynamics.

The growing demand for audio understanding is driving the need for more accurate and efficient methods to collect and label data. Traditional methods of manual annotation are time-consuming and often ineffective when dealing with diverse audio content. In this study, we explore the potential of an unsupervised audio tagging system that can learn from unlabelled data. Our approach utilizes a Variational Autoencoder to capture the underlying patterns in audio content and then employs a classification model to predict relevant labels. We tested this method using a large dataset of YouTube videos and compared its performance to a supervised baseline. The results show that the unsupervised system can generate relevant tags for audio content without any prior knowledge, making it a promising tool for large-scale data annotation initiatives.

The stability of diversity in natural ecosystems and biochemical reactions is influenced by random fluctuations in species abundance, leading to a possible phase transition between a disordered and an ordered state. This phase transition is characterized by a sudden change in behavior when a specific concentration threshold is reached. Our study explores the connection between random fluctuations and system stability by analyzing the stability of a model chemical reaction network subject to random fluctuations in species abundance. This model, inspired by the lambda-phage infection process, demonstrates that random fluctuations can lead to a possible phase transition between a stable and an unstable state. Our findings indicate that the reaction network is stable for a wide range of parameter settings, but random fluctuations can cause a sudden shift to an unstable state when the reaction rate exceeds a critical threshold.

We investigate the properties of a network that undergoes fragmentation after the removal of a single node, focusing on the relationship between the resulting cascade size and network structure. Our theoretical model allows us to derive an equation that describes the relationship between avalanche size and degree, which we validate through simulations using both synthetic and real-world networks. Additionally, we demonstrate how the derived equation can be employed to estimate the degree distribution of a network based on early fragmentation data.

Despite the recent breakthroughs in individual sentence understanding, developing comprehensive discourse models remains a significant challenge due to the inherent complexity of discourse structure. This study proposes a novel framework for analyzing discourse structure, which leverages the strengths of both the tree structure and linear sequence models. By incorporating a cross-attention mechanism, our approach enables the alignment of individual sentences with their contributions to the surrounding discourse. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model through experiments on two tasks: discourse parsing and inference. Notably, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on both tasks with minimal training data.

A novel approach to seismic wave propagation has been developed using the parallel finite-difference method on unstructured grids. This method leverages the open-source OpenFDM solver, which is optimized for multi-core and GPU processing. To enhance the method's efficiency, anisotropy is incorporated using the stress-projection technique, while a new absorbing boundary condition is implemented to minimize wave reflection. The method's performance is demonstrated through various numerical examples, including a 2D and 3D test case with an anisotropic model. The results show that the new absorbing boundary condition achieves a significant reduction in reflections, with only a minor increase in computational costs. Furthermore, the use of parallelism and GPU acceleration can save up to 90% of computational resources, making it an effective solution for complex seismic modeling tasks.

The process of a droplet breaking apart into smaller parts is studied through computer simulations.  A droplet with a certain level of surface energy is placed on a flat surface and collides with a stationary droplet.  The initial shape of the droplet is carefully controlled to create a predictable pattern of how it splits apart.  A new type of butterfly-like breakup is identified, which is not seen in other similar scenarios.  Further analysis shows that this new type of breakup occurs when the droplet is initially placed at a certain angle, resulting in a unique pattern of how it splits apart.  Theoretical calculations are able to accurately predict the likelihood of this new type of breakup happening based on the size and angle of the droplet.

The rapid growth of IoT devices necessitates a more efficient approach to traffic management, which can be achieved by isolating IoT traffic from the traditional network management paradigm. Our proposed solution utilizes SDN's centralized control to segment the network into IoT and non-IoT traffic domains, achieving improved performance, resource utilization, and enhanced network services.

The formation of planets is closely linked to the structure of the protoplanetary disk, specifically its density and temperature patterns. The presence of a planet can cause the disk to warp and create areas of high and low pressure, influencing the formation of a disk atmosphere. The shape of the planet's orbit plays a significant role in the complexity of the flow patterns, with the potential to create multiple vortices and strong turbulence. The study of the flow around a Saturn-mass planet at a distance of 30 astronomical units has revealed a complex disk atmosphere with multiple features, including a strong jet and a series of vortices. The analysis of the flow suggests that the planet's gravitational influence is significant, with the potential to create a strong jet and a disk atmosphere. The study's findings have implications for the formation of planets and the potential for future missions to detect and study the disk atmosphere.

Geometric deep learning models have been developed in Euclidean, hyperbolic, and symmetric positive definite spaces. We examine the similarities and differences between these models, specifically how they handle the geometry of data, and their practical applications. Our results show that models based on symmetric positive definite spaces consistently outperform those based on Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces across various tasks. This is because the geometry of data is often better represented by symmetric positive definite spaces than the other three options. We also found that models based on Euclidean spaces tend to perform well when the data is linearly separable, but struggle with non-linearly separable data. On the other hand, models based on hyperbolic spaces tend to perform well with data that has a hierarchical structure, but struggle with data that doesn't fit this pattern.

The existing hydrogen transportation network is primarily designed for natural gas, with the majority of it capable of being repurposed for low-pressure hydrogen pipelines. This includes 70% of the hydrogen backbone infrastructure, with a further 20% consisting of high-pressure pipelines that can be upgraded for the same purpose. Additionally, 8% of the infrastructure requires upgrading to high-pressure capacity, and 2% of the infrastructure needs to be replaced entirely. A comprehensive study of pipeline connections and capacity utilization reveals that a hydrogen pipeline system with a high-pressure pressure drop of 60 bar can supply 60% of the required hydrogen for the eastern United States, with the remaining 40% potentially met through local production. This analysis also shows that a hydrogen pipeline system with a high-pressure pressure drop of 70 bar can supply 80% of the required hydrogen for the eastern United States, with the remaining 20% potentially met through local production.

A recent study of solar observations has provided new insights into the relationship between the Sun's surface magnetic field and its subsurface field. The researchers analyzed data from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, specifically looking at how the subsurface field changes with depth. The study focused on a specific region of the Sun and compared its magnetic field to that of a similar area on the solar surface. The results showed a significant difference in the subsurface field, with a 180-degree difference in the direction of the magnetic field compared to the surface. This difference was observed at depths of 1.03 to 1.07 solar radii. The researchers also found that the strength of the subsurface field was about 1.5 times weaker than the surface field. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of the Sun's magnetic field and its behavior.

In integrated photonics, topological photonics has been utilized to produce squeezed light. However, the existing methods rely on complex photonic crystal lattices that are difficult to manufacture. In this research, we have developed a new approach to create a topological phase using a simple nanobeam waveguide with a single curved structure. This leads to the emergence of a topological phase and a zero-mode boundary, resulting in the generation of squeezed light. Our findings demonstrate the potential of nanobeam waveguides in producing squeezed light with minimal fabrication complexity.

This research introduces a novel trajectory planning technique for drones that ensures flight safety and efficiency in the face of sensor noise and environmental uncertainty. The proposed method employs a trajectory optimization approach that balances multiple objectives, including minimizing time, fuel consumption, and the risk of collision. The authors successfully tested their method in a real-world setting, comparing its performance to a conventional polynomial trajectory method. Notably, their method outperformed the comparison by reducing completion time by approximately 8.3%.

This paper explores the properties of a novel class of codes known as F_q-linear additive conjugacy codes. It provides a detailed enumeration of these codes for a given length n and F_q. Furthermore, the study calculates the number of F_q-linear additive subfields within these conjugacy codes and establishes a connection between the additive code's dimension and the number of its subfields. The research also examines the relationship between the additive conjugacy codes and the subfields of F_q[x] by defining a corresponding algebraic code over F_q[x]. The paper concludes with an analysis of the dual of the additive conjugacy code and its relationship to the conjugacy codes of a specific group, ultimately identifying a link between the two through the use of finite groups.

The physics community has long been a collaborative environment, where researchers freely share their findings and engage with the public, including students from various backgrounds. This exposure to industry professionals and alumni can be particularly beneficial in helping HEP students transition smoothly into careers outside of research. To foster this understanding, the University of Melbourne has established a program that invites HEP students to meet and learn from individuals who have successfully transitioned into industry roles. This initiative aims to provide valuable insights and guidance, making it easier for HEP students to consider non-academic paths after their studies.

The angular correlation between the b-quark and the W boson from top quark decay provides a sensitive indicator of W boson polarization. In a study of t-tbar events at the LHC, we employed a technique to measure this correlation using the CMS detector at 13 TeV. The results were obtained from a dataset of 36.3 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions. By comparing the observed data to various predictions, we determined that the angular distribution was consistent with the standard model of particle physics.

We've derived a set of novel sum rules for the ξ-moments of the twist-3 D-meson distribution amplitudes, specifically in terms of the ξ-moments of the π and K mesons, as well as the ρ and ω vector mesons. These sum rules are based on the concept of generalized parton distributions and provide a clear, process-independent connection between the D-meson distribution amplitudes and those of other mesons. The resulting sum rules can be used to break the degeneracy among D-meson distribution amplitudes, ultimately shedding light on their physical forms.

In 2018, researchers introduced a power hypergraph model and demonstrated a connection between its eigenvalues and the maximum signed subgraph count of the hypergraph. This connection led to a re-evaluation of the hypergraph's Laplacian eigenvalues, and our study extends this relationship to general weighted hypergraphs. Our findings show that the previously established eigenvalue-eigenvector relationship in power hypergraphs was incorrect, and our study corrects this error by broadening its scope to all weighted hypergraphs. This discovery resolves several previously reported errors in the literature, and our study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the Laplacian eigenvalues of weighted hypergraphs.

This study presents a novel method for determining the relative positions of two satellites in orbit, utilizing only inter-satellite measurements. The proposed approach is based on the Bayesian filtering technique, incorporating the Extended Kalman Filter, to estimate the orbit of a reference satellite and subsequently calculate the satellite's localisation in both orbit geometrical and cartesian coordinates. The research also compares the accuracy of this method with a baseline that combines inter-satellite and ground station data, revealing a high degree of consistency. Furthermore, the impact of various factors, including the number of measurements and the signal noise level, on the estimation process is examined.

The exoplanet XO-3b, a hot Jupiter, is notable for its unusually short orbital period decrease, which is not easily explained by conventional theories on how stars and planets interact in terms of tidal interactions. Our research aims to investigate the cause of this rapid orbital decay, which is significantly faster than what would be expected from standard models. By analyzing the XO-3b system using data from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS), we have been able to determine its orbital period with greater precision, finding a value of 0.0379877 days. Our analysis also reveals that the planet's orbital decrease is occurring at a rate of 1.78 microseconds per year, which is consistent with previous findings. Our research suggests that the planet's orbital decay is likely the result of the host star's magnetic activity, which is caused by its rotation and leads to the transfer of angular momentum to the planet. Our results also imply that the planet's tidal interactions with the host star are more efficient than previously thought, which is consistent with recent theories on how stars and planets interact in terms of tidal interactions.

The challenge of calibrating complex astrophysical experiments is a critical one, particularly when dealing with the vast amounts of data generated by experiments like the Dark Energy Survey and the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope. To tackle this issue, researchers have developed a novel Bayesian approach that incorporates machine learning techniques. By leveraging the strengths of both methods, this approach has the potential to significantly improve calibration precision and minimize systematic errors. The proposed technique involves a two-stage process. Initially, a machine learning model is trained to identify and characterize the relationships between the calibration parameters and the experiment's data. The resulting model is then used to inform a Bayesian calibration algorithm, which can be either a traditional maximum likelihood estimator or a more advanced method that incorporates prior knowledge and improves the experiment's overall calibration. The effectiveness of this approach has been successfully demonstrated through its application to the Dark Energy Survey's redshift space distortion measurement pipeline.

We establish a mathematical connection between the zeroth genus Gromov-Witten theory of projective bundles in the context of equivariant quantum Schubert geometry. This connection reveals that such projective bundles are defined by their underlying vector bundles, which can be further encapsulated in a specific matrix form. This finding allows us to derive a recursive formula for the zeroth genus Gromov-Witten invariants of projective bundles, and we also identify a corresponding formula for the number of points on a Lagrangian correspondence within the equivariant Gromov-Witten theory.

We establish asymptotic expressions for the central values of Rankin-Selberg L-functions for general weights m, involving a Dirichlet character and self-twisting of cusp automorphic representations of GL2 over the rational numbers. This method yields a novel approach to obtaining the analytic rank of an individual cusp eigenform.

In clinical trials, researchers often analyze continuous outcomes by comparing mean differences between treatment groups. However, this approach may be insufficient when outcomes have limitations, such as when patients are only measured at specific times. To address this issue, we propose a novel method for constrained longitudinal data analysis that leverages natural cubic splines to model outcomes and accounts for bounded data. Our approach is based on a two-part model that separates bounded and unbounded components, allowing for more accurate estimates and inference. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness through simulations and a real-world example using data from the PROFESS trial.

We introduce CRAWLING, a probabilistic and distributed routing algorithm for
WLAN mesh networks that considers the behavior of wireless channels and node
mobility by taking into account the uncertainty of channel state and node
position. CRAWLING's routing process is based on the expected transmission count
(ETC) metric, which estimates the likelihood of a route's success. The algorithm
uses a hop-by-hop approach to estimate the reliability of each link by calculating
the probability of packet loss, then adjusts the ETC metric accordingly. CRAWLING
also incorporates a probabilistic mechanism to detect and correct errors in the
ETC values. Our simulation results demonstrate that CRAWLING outperforms
existing routing algorithms in terms of packet delivery rate, average delay, and
average transmission count.

This study compares stochastic gradient descent with flat-minima optimization techniques, namely random weight perturbation and weight averaging, in their ability to enhance scalability in optimization processes. We examine the interplay between these methods' parameters and their effects on convergence speed, and investigate how they interact with various optimization algorithms, including simple and advanced variants. Our analysis also considers the impact of batch sizes and initial weight perturbations on the performance of these techniques, and we provide empirical evidence of their effectiveness across different scenarios.

A parametric frequency selective limiter is a compact, low-loss signal attenuator that can be triggered by a strong signal at a different frequency, operating in a broad frequency range from 1.3 to 20 GHz. This device offers low insertion loss and high power threshold levels, making it suitable for a wide range of applications. When triggered, the device's insertion loss significantly increases to block high power signals, while remaining in a low-loss state without an input. This device is particularly useful for applications requiring low-loss signal conditioning, such as satellite communications and remote sensing systems.

We're examining the impact of a time-dependent quarantine measure on epidemic trends, using a mathematical model that accounts for the behavior of infected and isolated individuals. The model's dynamics are influenced by the rate at which people are quarantined, as well as the rate at which they are released. Through a series of analytical and numerical studies, we're investigating the effects of this time-dependent quarantine on the behavior of the epidemic model. We've found that the introduction and removal of quarantine can create multiple waves of infection, and that the initial size and final disappearance of these waves can be controlled by adjusting the timing of the quarantine measure. Furthermore, we're exploring how the behavior of the epidemic model is influenced by the rate at which people are quarantined, as well as the rate at which they are released.

In this research, we investigate the effectiveness of integrating sentence context and structural characteristics derived from dependency trees for improving supervised term-matching tasks. Experimental evaluations were conducted using English and German texts, with a focus on two prominent semantic matching methods, including the vector-based approach and the pattern-based approach. The results demonstrate that combining context and structural features consistently enhances supervised term-matching performance, particularly when utilizing the vector-based method. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that certain English and German corpora present unique challenges, such as data sparsity and imbalance issues, which our proposed approach can effectively address.

We investigate the asymptotic behavior of the probability of a specific cluster in a d-dimensional Poisson Boolean model with increasing intensity, $\lambda$, as it approaches infinity. The focus is on the cluster centered at the origin, which is defined by the condition that all neighboring clusters are significantly farther away. The study reveals that the probability of this cluster, $\mathcal{P}_\lambda$, diminishes to zero at a rate of $1/\lambda^{d/2}$ when $d\geq 2$. Furthermore, we establish that the probability of the cluster being empty, $\mathcal{F}_\lambda$, also approaches zero at a rate of $1/\lambda^{(d+2)/2}$ when $d\geq 2$. The study also provides a lower bound for the probability of the cluster being finite, $\mathcal{P}_\lambda$, which is proportional to $\lambda^{-d/2}$. The results are derived from a detailed analysis of the asymptotic behavior of the probability of the cluster being finite, which is based on the study of the expected number of infinite clusters in a Poisson Boolean model with bounded clusters. The study also provides a lower bound for the probability of the cluster being finite, which is proportional to $\lambda^{-d/2}$. The results are further extended to a more general class of Poisson point processes with bounded clusters.

This study explores the equilibrium solutions of a rapidly rotating, two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equation in both barotropic and baroclinic states. These equilibrium solutions are essential for understanding the early stages of stellar evolution, particularly in the context of protoplanetary disks. The analysis reveals that stable equilibrium states exist for both rotating and non-rotating conditions, and that these states can be approximated by a simplified equation. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that these equilibrium states can be used to model the early stages of stellar formation, and that these models can be applied to real-world scenarios. The research also shows that these equilibrium states can be used to model the early stages of stellar formation, and that these models can be used to calculate the mass of the disk.

The structure scalars in the context of the Lema\^{\i}tre-Tolman-Bondi spacetime have been thoroughly researched. Conversely, the corresponding study for the generalized Lema\^{\i}tre-Tolman-Bondi spacetime remains an unexplored area. This paper aims to fill this gap by investigating the structure scalars within the generalized spacetime, providing a comprehensive understanding of their properties and behavior.

In a multipartite system, we investigate the relationship between nonlocal subsets and the local concealment of information. We demonstrate that in a $k$-partite state, hiding subsets with a size of $k$ or greater is impossible locally. Conversely, we show that in a $k$-partite system, hiding subsets with a maximum size of $k-1$ can always be achieved locally. This is achieved by constructing a specific type of multipartite state for each subset size. Furthermore, our results are applied to the field of quantum key distribution, providing a more refined understanding of the local security of key distribution protocols.

This study introduces a novel framework for identifying regions of interest on websites based on users' visual attention. A large dataset of unlabeled web pages was collected and annotated, and a model was trained to predict attention regions using a multilabel classification approach. The model's effectiveness was evaluated by comparing its attention predictions with the actual areas of interest on web pages. The results show that the model's attention predictions are highly accurate, achieving an F1-score of 0.754 on a validation set. Furthermore, the model's ability to learn from unlabeled data and its robustness to varying image sizes were also demonstrated. The study's findings have significant implications for developing automated systems that can identify areas of interest on websites and improve the user experience.

A groundbreaking, 2-bit transmissive Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS) element is introduced, significantly enhancing the phase modulation of reflected electromagnetic waves. This innovative design combines two 1-bit RIS elements with a precise phase-shifting mechanism, allowing for a vast, continuous phase range. Rigorous analysis of the RIS's transmission characteristics is conducted, and its potential applications in enhancing communication systems are explored.

In offline reinforcement learning, policies are developed without additional data beyond a given dataset. A common approach involves formulating the problem as a linear program, which can be solved efficiently using standard solvers. However, this method's efficiency relies on the size of the dataset, which can be impractical for larger datasets. To address this, we propose an algorithm that uses a small number of random features to reformulate the problem as a kernelized linear quadratic regulator, and then applies a gradient-based optimization technique. This approach has the potential to significantly reduce the computational requirements of offline reinforcement learning.

In this research, we establish a connection between the homotopy theory of
higher inductive types and traditional higher inductive spaces. Our main
finding is that a higher inductive type can be mapped to a sequence of
sets where the connectivity levels match the dimensions of the type, much
like the relationship between homotopy groups and connectedness in
classical topology. We also demonstrate how to translate the suspension
operation on homotopy types to a construction within type theory using
higher inductive types.

We have conducted a detailed study of the supermassive black hole (SMBH) in the galaxy M81, using a combination of high-resolution imaging and spectroscopy from the Hubble Space Telescope and the Wide-Field Camera 3. Our analysis of the SMBH's motion reveals a velocity offset of 20 km/s from its host galaxy, suggesting that the SMBH is dynamically out of place. This is consistent with the SMBH being a recent or past merger remnant, and our findings are supported by a number of independent observations.

In the context of the three-body problem, our study focuses on periodic solutions that lack collinear configurations. Specifically, we've developed a new method to address the question of whether such solutions exist under a given set of conditions. This approach is applied to a problem involving a satellite and a planet, with the goal of determining the existence of periodic orbits that could be used as a solution to satellite control issues.

A novel approach to fluorescence imaging is proposed, leveraging the spatial correlation of light emitted from multiple fluorescent sources that are sufficiently close together.  The resulting method, referred to as near-field fluorescence imaging, can be implemented using a commercial microscope and does not necessitate any additional hardware or software modifications.  Theoretical models predict that when multiple fluorescent molecules are present within the diffraction limit of a single image frame, the resulting light emission will exhibit a unique statistical correlation that can be utilized to generate an in-depth image of the fluorescent sources.  The accuracy of this method was experimentally validated by comparing it with the results obtained from a highly sensitive super-resolution microscopy technique called super-resolution ground-state recovery microscopy.  The findings of this study indicate that near-field fluorescence imaging has the potential to be a valuable tool for the rapid and cost-effective analysis of biological samples at the nanoscale.

User preference modeling is a critical task in e-commerce, enabling personalized recommendations. However, existing models primarily focus on individual items, neglecting the complex relationships between items. Moreover, most models rely on a single, isolated user behavior pattern, overlooking the diverse range of behaviors and their interactions. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework that simultaneously captures item relationships and comprehensive user behavior patterns. Our framework, Reciprocal Modeling of User Preference (RMUP), utilizes a graph neural network to model item relationships and a hierarchical attention mechanism to represent user behavior. We demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms baseline methods in both offline and online tests.

Graph representation learning has become increasingly significant in the realm of computer vision and graph mining. Recent studies have shown that self-supervised learning can be an effective approach to graph representation learning, particularly through node representation learning. This paper introduces a novel self-supervised graph learning method that utilizes geodesic similarity to create node representations. By incorporating a geodesic similarity module into the graph, we can generate more informative node representations. Our method, GeoSim, has been tested on various graph benchmarks and outperformed other state-of-the-art approaches in node classification tasks.

This paper explores the potential of uplink grant-free access in massive machine-type communications, utilizing non-orthogonal sequences to boost performance. Theoretical analysis is conducted to determine the optimal sequence length, and simulation results demonstrate the superiority of grant-free access over traditional orthogonal multiplexing in terms of both throughput and latency.

We introduce a novel factorization approach, called Decoder-Expander Based Factorisation, which efficiently uncovers the underlying sparse codes from linear measurements obtained through channels affected by noise. This algorithm builds on the existing Decoder-Expander Based Merging method and offers a more streamlined and faster alternative. Notably, it maintains the robustness to randomization inherent in the original Merging technique, while significantly reducing its computational complexity.

This study introduces a novel approach to differentiable adversarial data augmentation, leveraging spatial transformer networks to address the limitations of existing methods. By incorporating differentiable transformations, our method enables the precise localization of adversarial patches, allowing for more effective and efficient augmentation. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on the task of domain adaptation in semantic segmentation, comparing it to state-of-the-art augmentation techniques. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing methods, yielding superior performance on multiple datasets, particularly when limited data is available.

This paper delves into the behavior of spatial and 2-local derivations within infinite-dimensional self-adjoinable matrix-valued map algebras, specifically examining their construction and properties, as well as the Gelfand-Naimark-Segal (GNS) representation associated with these derivations. Furthermore, it investigates the behavior of 2-local derivations in relation to the compact operators acting on infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.

Berry's phase is a geometric concept that arises from the motion of a system's Hamiltonian in parameter space, and its associated topological properties are of significant interest. In this study, we investigate the geometric structure of Berry's phase in a two-level system with a time-dependent, off-diagonal electric field that generates a level crossing in energy. By deriving an analytical solution to the Schrödinger equation, we examine the dynamics of the system's dipole moment and calculate the Berry phase, and our findings reveal a distinct change in the system's topology at the crossing point. Furthermore, we analyze the influence of the system's parameters on Berry's phase and demonstrate that the phase exhibits a nontrivial topological structure that is characterized by a monopole.

We investigate compactons in spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensates with spin-orbit coupling, which are described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation with a Zeeman field. The results show that the compactons become more feasible under a specific magnetic field, enabling the creation of localized matter waves with a spin degree of freedom. Our findings open up possibilities for studying compactons in spinor BECs and exploring their potential applications in quantum information processing.

We've calculated the ratios of decay widths for certain $B$ meson decays using the HQET effective theory, specifically focusing on the $B_{(s)}\to D_{(s)}$ transitions. Our calculations, up to the next-to-leading order in the HQET expansion, take into account the effects of charm quark mass corrections and utilize the $1/m_Q$ expansion method. The results show significant deviations from the expected $1/m_Q$ behavior in the HQET limit, particularly in the ratio of decay widths, and we have also estimated the size of the next-to-next-to-leading order corrections.

This research explores the orbit space resulting from a Lie group's action on a smooth manifold and investigates its implications for functions and approximation. We establish that the orbit space is a smooth manifold and demonstrate that the action induces a continuous homomorphism from the Lie group to the continuous automorphisms of the orbit space. Furthermore, we examine various properties of the orbit space, including its topological properties, continuity of functions, and approximation capabilities. Specifically, we show that the orbit space is a Fréchet space and that the space of continuous functions on the orbit space is isometrically isomorphic to the space of continuous functions on the original manifold.

A future muon collider could serve as an advanced tool to study heavy axion-like particles (hALPs) that interact with fermions, complementing existing research at lepton colliders and the proposed FCC-ee. The machine would allow for a comprehensive exploration of the parameter space of these particles, particularly in scenarios where they interact with electrons or muons, offering a significant advantage over other collider options. The study of hALPs at a muon collider would be facilitated by the observation of muon disappearance, offering a unique detection method. The analysis of muon collisions at a 100 TeV muon collider would be feasible, even in scenarios where the center-of-mass energy is below the muon mass.

This paper introduces MetaSys, a flexible framework that streamlines the implementation and assessment of cross-layer hardware techniques. By leveraging a meta-programming approach, MetaSys enables users to efficiently create and connect various hardware components, encompassing both digital logic and analog circuits, across multiple layers of hardware. The framework's design incorporates a hierarchical abstraction that distinguishes between system-level architecture, hardware components, and physical components, allowing for a clear and customizable implementation structure. Through a real-world example, we demonstrate that MetaSys can significantly reduce the effort required to design and verify complex hardware systems, yielding a notable 3.5 times reduction in code size and 2.5 times reduction in design time.

In recent years, deep learning has gained significant traction in the field of biotechnology, with applications such as CHO-K1 suspension growth analysis gaining attention. However, the lack of large datasets hinders the effectiveness of deep learning in biotech. This study proposes a novel Twin-VAE model that leverages transfer learning to address this issue. The Twin-VAE model consists of two interconnected VAEs: a data VAE that learns the underlying patterns of the training data, and a prior VAE that learns the distribution of the data's latent space. The Twin-VAE model is then used to generate new data that can be employed for transfer learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the Twin-VAE model by successfully applying it to the CHO-K1 suspension growth dataset, achieving a 10% improvement in model performance compared to a traditional VAE.

We've developed a novel approach to prove that a weak solution to the nonlinear dynamic boundary problem \begin{equation}\left\{\begin{array}{lll} u' + \alpha \Delta u = 0, \quad \mbox{in} \ (0,T)\times \Omega,\\
u(\cdot,t) = 0, \quad \mbox{on} \ (0,T), \quad \partial_{\nu} u(\cdot,t) = 0, \quad \mbox{on} \ ( \partial \Omega \times [0,T] ), \end{array}\right. \end{equation} is in fact a strong solution. This is achieved by transforming the problem into an equivalent parabolic system of equations, which can be solved using a fixed point argument. Our method is adaptable to a broader class of dynamic boundary problems.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are a fundamental component of natural language processing, but they can be challenging to optimize due to the vanishing or exploding gradient problem. To address this issue, we propose a novel architecture called the Fourier Recurrent Unit (FRU) that utilizes a Fourier basis to decompose recurrent states, facilitating the propagation of gradients. Our Fourier analysis reveals that the traditional RNN model acts as a linear system, and we demonstrate that modifying the model to incorporate non-linear Fourier components improves its capacity to learn complex patterns. Experimental results demonstrate that the FRU outperforms standard RNNs on a range of tasks, including language modeling, sentiment analysis, and text classification.

In the active pure exploration problem, we seek to identify the most frequent item within a set of items, where each item belongs to a specific category and is drawn according to a distribution. The key distinction between active pure exploration and other pure exploration problems lies in the adaptive and informed approach, where we can query items based on the obtained information. The online setting is further distinguished from the generative setting, where we can only query items in the online scenario. We present a novel algorithm for the online active pure exploration problem, which provides a regret bound of $O(T^{4/3})$ and demonstrates an improved offline bound of $O(\log M)$, where T represents the total number of queries and M denotes the number of items.

We have developed a model to study the behavior of attosecond electrons in a plasma wave, with a focus on how their spin direction influences their collective motion. By analyzing the dynamics of spin-dependent electron interactions, we have identified key factors that affect the attoseond electrons' path and their final energy distribution upon reaching the plasma-vacuum interface. Our research reveals that the spin direction of these electrons plays a crucial role in determining their trajectory, and thus, their final energy distribution upon reaching the interface. Furthermore, we have found that the spin-orbit interaction in the attoseond electrons' motion can be controlled by adjusting the spin polarization of these electrons, the density of the plasma, and the distance between the plasma and the interface. Our study provides a new approach for manipulating the spin-orbit interaction in high-energy electron beams, with potential applications in fields such as ultrafast electron microscopy and spintronics.

This paper explores the underlying dynamics of vital field driven mutations within the framework of a vital field theory. By establishing a connection between these mutations and classical mutations, we derive a mathematical expression that links vital field driven mutations to classical mutations. We then investigate the characteristics of these mutations, including their impact on entropy, birth and death rates, and the distribution of population sizes. Our findings indicate that vital field driven mutations result in increased entropy, divergent population sizes, and a Gaussian distribution. Furthermore, we derive an equation that relates the mean square birth and death rates to the square of the vital field strength.

The rapidly growing availability of data on Science, Technology, and Innovation (STI) across various sources worldwide has created a pressing need for a system that enables data interoperability. This interoperability is crucial for gaining a deeper understanding of the broader STI ecosystems, which in turn can foster innovation and drive sustainable development. Achieving this interoperability necessitates the development of standards for data exchange, including metadata standards that facilitate the discovery, integration, and visualization of STI data. This paper presents an open-source metadata standard called C3DISCO, which enables the creation of a unified, interoperable landscape of STI data from diverse sources.

Applications that use the Android NDK often rely on sensitive functions that expose crucial information about the device and its surroundings. This "side-channel leak" can lead to significant breaches of user privacy and potentially expose sensitive data. Our research reveals that these leaks are widespread in popular Android apps and allows attackers to exploit them to steal sensitive information such as GPS locations. We propose a method to detect and prevent these leaks by identifying potentially vulnerable functions and analyzing their input and output patterns. Our tool, NDKLeak, has been shown to be effective in detecting these leaks in real-world apps and can be used to prevent them from occurring.

This research introduces a novel approach to examining Ethereum ego networks through time. We present an efficient method to construct and analyze ego networks of Ethereum addresses over time, enabling the identification of connections and transactions. The proposed framework facilitates the application of various social network analysis techniques to these dynamic ego networks. We demonstrate the utility of our approach by applying temporal ego network analysis to investigate money laundering through wire-transfer schemes on the Ethereum blockchain.

The LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ (LAO/STO) interface, a model oxide heterostructure, has garnered significant attention for its unique properties. These properties stem from the interplay between the substrate and the interface, which can be altered by external stimuli, such as light, to create new functionalities. In this study, we investigated the impact of light on the LAO/STO interface, and found that it can induce a significant increase in the number of charge carriers, as well as modify the interface's magnetic behavior. Our findings suggest that the interface's response to light is linked to the emergence of highly mobile charge carriers, which can then interact with the interface's magnetic properties, leading to new behaviors.

We have developed an algorithm that can determine the provability of a wide range of first-order formulas within the framework of pomset and timed pomset logic. This algorithm's associated decision problem is known to be undecidable. Notably, our findings demonstrate that pomset logic's provability is computationally less complex than that of BV logic, which is known to be less complex than that of timed pomset logic. Additionally, our research has shown that pomset logic is more expressive than linear-time temporal logic. This algorithm's implementation is available in the Coq Proofs system.

The connection between Macdonald polynomials and the five-term relation discovered by Garsia and Mel'nikov is established through a general formula. This formula is derived from the five-term relation and leads to a specific equation for Macdonald polynomials, which in turn yields a new formula for the $\tau$-function of the q-difference operator of Macdonald polynomials.

A crucial factor in astronomical surveys is having redshift data available for source galaxies. This key piece of information enables researchers to categorize sources into distinct types, such as stars or galaxies, and facilitates the development of statistical models that can be used to analyze the universe. This study presents a novel method for estimating the redshift of galaxies using a combination of deep learning algorithms and photometric data. The approach, which involves training a convolutional neural network, has been tested using data from the Dark Energy Survey and yields results that are comparable to those obtained using traditional photometric methods. The findings indicate that the new approach can provide accurate redshift estimates for galaxies, even those without prior measurements, and can be used to create a more comprehensive and accurate dataset for analyzing the universe.

This paper presents a Bayesian decision support system to assess policy implications on operational costs. It utilizes a Markov chain model to simulate the daily behavior of a highway network, incorporating traffic flow and congestion. A linear regression model is employed to calculate the probability of congestion based on traffic patterns. A Bayesian estimator is utilized to determine the uncertainty in the estimated parameters. Users input different policy scenarios, and the system calculates the expected congestion level and corresponding costs using Monte Carlo simulations and Bayesian decision analysis. Users can choose between two cost models: a simple linear model and a more complex model accounting for traffic density. Our system is demonstrated using a section of the Pennsylvania Turnpike, illustrating how different policy scenarios affect costs.

We have developed a theoretical framework to investigate the QC-DMRG method's behavior in a two-electron system. Our analysis shows that, under specific conditions, the energy output from this method converges to a precise FCI energy value, resulting in exact energy eigenstates. This convergence is attributed to the method's ability to iteratively refine its description of the wavefunction, starting with an FCI state. Notably, the QC-DMRG method can be viewed as a variant of the FCI algorithm, with the former's iterative refinement process enabled by a non-zero imaginary time step. This approach is analogous to the imaginary time evolution method, with the two methods' time steps being directly proportional to each other. Our findings also indicate that, in certain scenarios, the QC-DMRG method can be considered an exact method, with the remaining errors stemming from numerical inaccuracies rather than the algorithm's inherent limitations.

We investigate a scenario in which a dark matter particle is a pseudo-Goldstone boson linked to a dark Higgs boson. This dark matter particle is a light, pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson resulting from a discrete dark gauge symmetry that is broken at a low scale. We analyze the implications of this setup on the muon's anomalous magnetic moment and dark matter relic abundance, finding that the dark matter particle's mass should fall within 50-300 MeV. We also consider the constraints imposed by direct detection experiments, dark matter detection by haloscopes, and the stability of the dark gauge symmetry, as well as the potential for dark matter to induce a late-time acceleration of the universe.

A groundbreaking approach to simulation has been developed, leveraging the capabilities of the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) to solve complex partial differential equations (PDEs) in coastal flooding simulations. This novel method boasts an impressive 100 times increase in computational efficiency over traditional approaches, while maintaining remarkably low 2% error rates. Moreover, FNO's ability to handle diverse scenarios and data sparsity makes it an ideal solution for large-scale coastal flooding simulations.

A successful joint analysis platform for CMB research, such as the Planck Collaboration model, is crucial but faces significant challenges including data sharing, software integration, and analysis standardization. To overcome these obstacles, this article outlines the key factors necessary for the development of a collaborative analytical framework that can facilitate progress in CMB research. It emphasizes the importance of community engagement, software compatibility, and reproducible results in the design and implementation of such a platform.

The reaction-diffusion model, a fundamental concept in understanding pattern formation in living systems, has been extensively studied. However, the role of complex networks in these phenomena remains a relatively unexplored area. This study focuses on the reaction-diffusion model applied to random scale-free networks, where the activator and inhibitor diffusion constants are independently adjustable. Our findings indicate that the activator diffusion constant significantly affects the conditions for the Turing instability. Furthermore, the Turing instability is more pronounced when the activator diffusion constant is lower than the inhibitor. This study also reveals that the Turing instability in scale-free networks is influenced by the network size and degree distribution exponent.

We investigate the impact of a phantom field on the properties of a simple $\phi^4$ theory in $3+1$ dimensions, where the phantom field shares the same kinetic energy as the fundamental scalar but has a different potential energy. The introduction of the phantom field breaks the conservation of the theory's supercurrents, which is a characteristic of the $|\phi|^4$ theory. We calculate the anomalous dimension of the supercurrent operator and find that it is finite in the ultraviolet limit, provided the ghost field does not dominate the theory.

Our research focuses on the optical properties of GaAs nanowires with varying core diameters, specifically examining their electronic and optical characteristics. We observed that the emission and excitation patterns were influenced by the size of the nanowire's core, with the most significant changes occurring when the energy gap was shifted from the quantized mass-limit regime to the confinement regime. We found that the confinement energy was highly dependent on the size of the nanowire's core, with the most significant changes occurring when the core diameter was reduced. Our results also showed that the emission and excitation patterns were highly sensitive to the size of the nanowire's core, with the most significant changes occurring when the core diameter was reduced. Our research provides valuable insights into the optical properties of GaAs nanowires with different core diameters, specifically in the context of the confinement regime.

To develop effective dialogue models that can adapt to an opponent's preferences, we need to improve their ability to infer those preferences from the dialogue context. However, collecting a large enough dataset to train models to do this is a difficult task. We propose a new approach that allows dialogue models to learn an opponent's preferences by actively asking questions during the dialogue and using the response to refine their understanding. We also propose a new evaluation metric that can be used to assess whether a model has successfully inferred the opponent's preferences. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of experiments in a simple restaurant booking dialogue setting and show that it outperforms existing methods in detecting the opponent's preferences.

We investigate the relationship between the string length and the tension scalar in a three-dimensional spacetime containing two distinct strings. The interaction between these strings leads to a specific constraint on the tension scalar, which must ensure that both strings' world sheets remain conformally invariant. This constraint is more stringent than the one-string condition, resulting in a more restrictive range for the scalar tension.

In the Online Blocking Problem, we create a partition of n items by pulling i + 1 items from the remaining unchosen set at each step, aiming to minimize the size of the unchosen set. This problem has practical applications in online social science research, where sampling methods are used. Our study shows that a greedy algorithm that selects items randomly from the remaining set produces a partition with an expected size of O(log n). This result is achieved by applying a pigeonhole design concept, which was previously only known to produce a worst-case partition with an upper bound of O(n^(1 - epsilon)) for a small epsilon > 0.

Using a combination of computational methods, we have analyzed the electronic properties of the Si/gamma-Al2O3 interface with different surface terminations. Our results show that the interface with the unpassivated Si surface exhibits a significant bandgap alignment, with the oxide side showing n-type behavior and the silicon side showing p-type behavior. However, the passivated interface shows a different behavior, with the oxide side showing p-type behavior and the silicon side showing n-type behavior. Our calculations also suggest that the interface with the oxygen-terminated Al2O3 surface exhibits a negative electron affinity, consistent with experimental findings.

We investigate the behavior of the Einstein-axion-dilaton system within a framework of conformal gravity. Our findings indicate that spacetimes exhibiting self-similar gravitational collapse can undergo continuous, irreversible evolution. This evolution is characterized by a decrease in the dilaton, leading to a suppression of internal transformations and spacetime dilation. Ultimately, the system converges to a stable, asymptotic state, marked by a Schwarzschild black hole devoid of axions and dilaton.

This research investigates the impact of dismantling shipping cartels on the European shipping industry, utilizing data from the 1970s to the 1990s and a combination of empirical and theoretical approaches. A novel, dynamic model of price competition among shipping companies has been developed to analyze the effects of breaking up existing shipping monopolies.
