The proposed system's architecture incorporates functionalities such as data storage, retrieval, and web interface access, while also allowing for seamless integration with external tools and an online interface. The development process, including challenges encountered, is discussed in detail. Ultimately, the performance of the developed system is evaluated by assessing its speed, efficiency, and overall performance.

The initial mass function (IMF) of stars has a significant impact on the chemical enrichment of the interstellar medium. A study of the galaxy's mass-luminosity relationship found that the IMF exhibits a systematic variation with mass and metallicity. This variation leads to a variation in the mass of stars produced, which in turn affects the galaxy's chemical enrichment. A model of galaxy evolution was developed to investigate the effect of the IMF variation on the galaxy's evolution. The model found that the IMF variation leads to a variation in the mass of stars produced, which in turn affects the galaxy's chemical enrichment. The model also found that the IMF variation leads to a variation in the galaxy's star formation rate, which in turn affects the galaxy's evolution. The model's results are consistent with observations of the galaxy's mass-luminosity relationship and the galaxy's chemical enrichment. The model's results also suggest that the IMF variation is a key factor in understanding the galaxy's evolution.

This paper presents a group-based sparse representation approach to improve the computational efficiency of dictionary learning methods. By clustering columns of an initial dictionary, we can simultaneously learn sparse codes and dictionaries, while enforcing sparsity on a group level. This method has two main advantages: it significantly reduces the number of sparse codes, and it can handle large datasets in a block-wise manner, making it suitable for dictionaries with a large number of columns. Additionally, our method can be applied to various clustering techniques, such as k-means, and it can be used to develop a novel clustering dictionary learning algorithm that combines group-wise sparsity and dictionary learning. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving group-wise sparse codes and dictionaries, and its applicability to clustering dictionary learning methods.

This study introduces a cutting-edge, real-time object detection system, which
combines the efficiency of the YOLOv4 framework with the power of a novel
REthinker block. This innovative block, featuring a dual structure, significantly
boosts the network's sensitivity to object classes. Our proposed approach yields
impressive results, outperforming YOLOv4 with its equivalent parameters and
outshining YOLOv7 with its smaller parameter size. Notably, our model surpasses
YOLOR with its custom activation function, achieving a new state-of-the-art on the
COCO test-dev set while maintaining real-time capabilities.

This research focuses on a specific class of block codes known as PAC, which includes algebraic decoding and has a sequential decoding process. The complexity of this sequential process can be estimated by determining the average number of necessary syndrome calculations. For a specific subset of PAC, called linear PAC, this calculation has been theoretically established using the code's minimum distance. However, for more general PAC, this calculation has been practically implemented through a computer-assisted method. The results show that both scenarios produce reasonable, albeit not necessarily optimal, estimates.

In online sequential recommendation, models are trained on a stream of user-item interactions and expected to make future recommendations. However, these models are hindered by the lack of available user-item interaction data, particularly for users with limited or no historical interaction records. To address this issue, we propose a new approach called MetaTL that utilizes a Transformer-based model to predict user-item interactions and leverage the learned patterns to improve the sequential recommendation process. By incorporating a meta-learning framework, MetaTL can adapt to new users and items without extensive training data, and it can also be trained on a large number of users and items to enhance the sequential recommendation model's predictive power. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in both user rating prediction and online sequential recommendation tasks.

This document serves as a white paper submitted to the US Department of Energy's Investigator- Led Program (ILP) proposal submission for the 2021 cycle. It outlines a set of research questions and scientific objectives in the area of ultra high energy cosmic ray physics. We present a case for a new experiment that could address these questions and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the field. This new experiment would have the capability to detect particles with energies above 100 EeV and potentially resolve several long-standing mysteries surrounding UHECRs.

A study on the effects of projectile impact on basalt targets was conducted using the iBAFFLE facility in France, employing a two-stage light gas gun to launch spherical projectiles with varying geometries and speeds up to 4.5 km/s. The results revealed that the enhancement factor for momentum increases with the projectile's size, reaching a value of around 3. The experiment's findings were then compared with theoretical predictions from the hydrocode code CTH, which showed good agreement when accounting for boundary conditions and material properties. However, the hydrocode struggled to accurately model the effects of the projectile's geometry on the enhancement factor, underscoring the need for further research into the underlying physical processes.

This research presents an innovative method for capturing high-resolution, distortion-free images of faces through windshields. The existing facial recognition systems heavily rely on clear, unobstructed images of the face, which are not feasible in real-world scenarios where windshields are present. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel approach that utilizes a Mertens Unrolled Network-based model to generate high-quality images of the face through windshades. The proposed method involves two stages: the first stage utilizes a convolutional neural network to generate a set of high-quality images of the face through windshades, and the second stage utilizes a convolutional neural network to refine the generated images and produce a single high-quality image of the face. The proposed method has been evaluated on a dataset of 1,000 images of the face through windshades, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in recovering high-quality, distortion-free images of the face through windshades. The proposed method has been shown to outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in this domain, and the code and dataset will be made publicly available for future research.

Distributing source code packages through a web interface can be beneficial for developers working with languages such as Perl, Ruby, or Python. However, the process of accessing and extracting these packages is often cumbersome and requires manual intervention. This article presents a web service called GitAnn that facilitates the distribution of Git repositories via online bookmarks. Developers can utilize GitAnn to easily retrieve and integrate packaged source code into their projects, and the service also allows them to track repository updates with features like RSS feeds and search queries.

In survival analysis, when incorporating a variable with missing data is desirable but the data is missing at random, inverse probability weighting is a well-established method for addressing the issue. This approach can be combined with a machine learning algorithm, such as a random forest, to handle the missing data and subsequently model the survival distribution. However, the challenge lies in accurately quantifying the uncertainty in the resulting estimates. This is particularly crucial when using complex models, as it is difficult to determine the impact of the missing data handling procedure on the model's accuracy. This study aims to address this issue by developing a method to quantify the uncertainty in the data handling procedure and subsequently propagate it through the machine learning model. This is achieved by using a machine learning algorithm, specifically a random forest, to handle the missing data and then employing a Bayesian bootstrap method to quantify the uncertainty in the resulting estimates. The proposed method is evaluated through simulation studies and applied to a real-world dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling the uncertainty in the data handling procedure.

A novel function is constructed from the derivative of the complete elliptic integral of the first kind. Utilizing its specific characteristics, specific bounds and asymptotic behaviors can be precisely determined. These findings surpass Alzer and Qiu's previously proposed conjectures, yielding tighter bounds. Moreover, the function's behavior is used to derive asymptotic series for the complete elliptic integral of the first kind, specifically for large and extreme values of the parameter k.

Recent advancements in machine learning have led to the development of powerful models capable of performing tasks previously thought to require human intelligence. However, the extent to which these models truly possess intelligence remains unclear, as they often struggle with common sense and exhibit biases such as overfitting to training data. This study investigates whether these models can learn to apply common sense by leveraging large-scale text datasets, and explores the potential for using this knowledge to improve decision-making in reinforcement learning tasks. The results show that these models can, with sufficient training, learn to apply common sense and outperform previous approaches, including those that integrated it with reinforcement learning. Notably, the models required only a small fraction of the examples needed for human learners to master the same skill, raising questions about the nature of intelligence and its relationship to learning. This finding also highlights the potential for using large-scale text datasets to improve the decision-making capabilities of machine learning models, and suggests that this knowledge could be used to improve the performance of machine learning models in a variety of tasks.

This research introduces AraNews, a substantial dataset of 10,000 authentic and 2,400 artificially altered Arabic news articles, along with their corresponding labels. Our primary objective is to develop and evaluate machine learning models capable of identifying and differentiating between manipulated and authentic news in the Arabic language. The dataset was created using a combination of news articles from reputable sources and artificially altered content generated through two distinct methods. The manipulation techniques employed include the removal of content and the addition of false information. The dataset is divided into four categories, each representing a different level of manipulation severity. The dataset is publicly available for use in research, and we present the results of baseline experiments utilizing both pre-trained and custom neural networks.

A widely-held misconception about an earlier finding by Shafarevich has led to an overestimation of the number of fields of a specific type that are essentially one-dimensional over a given field. This paper corrects the misconception and provides an accurate count of such fields.

In the context of the $T\bar T$ deformation, we investigate the correlation functions of qubits within a $d$-dimensional conformal field theory, specifically those with a $\mathbb Z_2$ symmetry. This symmetry arises from the presence of a fermionic operator, which is treated as a fundamental object rather than an excitation. The study reveals that the correlation functions of qubits do not necessarily decrease with distance, as expected in a $d$-dimensional space. However, when the qubits are placed in a $1$-dimensional space, the correlation functions do exhibit decay at high energy, consistent with the expectations of the $T\bar T$ theory.

In the context of focused crawling, selecting the most relevant URLs from search engine results is a crucial task. The Tree-Frontier algorithm is a well-known approach that utilizes a heuristic evaluation of URLs to prioritize them, but it can be computationally intensive. This paper presents an optimized version of Tree-Frontier, leveraging the benefits of a pre-trained neural network to streamline the URL assessment process. We also introduce an innovative method to assess the neural network's confidence level in its predictions, enabling the selection of the most suitable heuristic when the network is uncertain. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses the Tree-Frontier algorithm across various domains and scenarios.

Traditional process mining methods rely on event logs, but they have limitations when dealing with complex data. A new approach, called object-centric event data, represents interactions among multiple objects, such as emails, invoices, and orders. This type of data is crucial in real-world process analysis. However, it requires a new methodology to be effectively analyzed using process mining techniques. This paper introduces an object-centric process mining framework that leverages object relationships to derive event data. It also discusses the challenges and opportunities in applying this methodology to real-world problems.

We introduce a novel approach for seismic data recovery that utilizes a recursive technique to reconstruct high-quality seismic data from incomplete measurements. This method is based on the assumption that the measured data is a result of a sparse and stable seismic source, and is therefore resistant to noise and missing data. We have developed a versatile algorithm that can be applied to a wide range of problems, and is capable of recovering data from various types of measurements, including those affected by noise. We have tested the performance of our algorithm on both synthetic and real-world data and have found it to significantly outperform existing methods in terms of both recovery quality and computational efficiency.

A silicon metalen with a wide field of view and high bandwidth has been designed and built. This metalen features a broad focus span of 85 degrees and a high operating frequency of 20 GHz. It was constructed using a standard silicon-on-insulator foundry and can focus 20 GHz microwave signals in a beam. This metalen has a wide field of view and can work effectively with both small and large sources. It was also found that the metalen's performance was not significantly affected by its position.

The self-consistent distribution of electrons in a plasma can be accurately described by a Gaussian or exponential curve, which is determined by the plasma's ion density. This distribution is analogous to the electrostatic potential generated by ions in a plasma, and its characteristics can be used to derive the Poisson equation and equilibrium. The Poisson-Boltzmann equation, which accounts for ion distribution, can be solved analytically to provide a general expression for the electrostatic potential. This equation can be further applied to various plasma scenarios, including spherical and cylindrical geometries, and can be used to calculate the electrostatic potential and the radius of the electron group. This approach can also be extended to the study of non-ideal plasmas, which exhibit non-linear behavior, and can be used to derive the Poisson-Nernst-Planck equation, which accounts for non-ideal effects.

We investigate the stability of higher-dimensional Schwarzschild black holes and circular null geodesics by analyzing quasinormal frequencies and principal Lyapunov exponents. Our findings show that the imaginary components of these frequencies align with the principal Lyapunov exponent for geodesics in the stable region. Conversely, in the unstable region, imaginary parts of frequencies are on the same side for geodesics and scalar fields. Furthermore, a phase transition exists at the Lyapunov exponent's zero crossing, which is the same point where frequency components align.

The search for a common directional distribution of pulsars in the universe is a key objective of the pulsar timing array collaboration. However, the lack of evidence for such correlations may indicate that the array is not sensitive to them, which could be due to inadequate filtering of noise. In this context, the primary focus should be on the relationship between the sensitivity of the array and the frequency of the pulsar signals. Notably, the most sensitive pulsars are those with lower spin frequencies, which is a characteristic that is independent of their spatial distribution.

The GM-MDS conjecture, which pertains to 2-MDS codes, has been a subject of significant research in recent years. This study aims to extend this conjecture to a broader class of codes, specifically algebraic geometry codes. We demonstrate that the direct extension of the GM-MDS conjecture is not applicable to all fields, as it holds true over finite fields. Furthermore, we establish the primary conditions under which the GM-MDS system can be generalized to a wide range of fields, and provide examples to illustrate these conditions. Additionally, we identify a specific instance where the GM-MDS system is not extendable to a wide range of fields.

Given a function φ on the unit circle and a matrix A, we define the matrix-valued truncated Toeplitz operator TφA and show that its kernel function can be expressed as a sum of the product of φ and the kernel of a scalar-valued truncated Toeplitz operator and the kernel of A, with its entries also expressed as a sum of products of φ and the kernels of scalar-valued truncated Toeiltz operators.

In a scenario where the sender has limited knowledge of the signal's distribution, she attempts to convince the receiver by offering a sequence of rewards. The receiver, aware of the signal's distribution but uncertain of the sender's strategy, must decide whether to accept or decline each offer based on her assessment of the sender's intentions. This interaction bears resemblance to a situation where a loan officer evaluates a loan applicant's creditworthiness, a situation where the lender is typically unaware of the specific circumstances surrounding the application. This problem is referred to as the non-determined signaling game and is analyzed within a Bayesian framework. It is demonstrated that the sender can implement any dominant strategy through a carefully designed sequence of rewards, provided that the sender places a sufficiently high value on the outcome that is preferred by the receiver. This result is achieved by employing a technique that involves the sender persuading the receiver by offering a sequence of rewards, where the sender's strategy is contingent on the receiver's prior assessment of the signal's distribution.

Unsupervised Anomaly Detection under Domain Shift Conditions, denoted by UAD-S, is a significant challenge in the field of anomaly detection. It involves training an anomaly detection model on a source domain with labeled data and then testing it on a target domain with no labeled data. The goal is to adapt the model to the target domain's distribution without prior knowledge of its anomalies. The model's performance is typically evaluated using metrics such as AUC, F1-score, and Recall. However, these metrics are insufficient to capture the impact of contextual changes between the source and target domains. This paper proposes a new evaluation framework for UAD-S that considers the effects of contextual changes, which can be categorized into two types: gradual and abrupt changes. The proposed framework assesses the model's performance in both scenarios and provides a more comprehensive understanding of its performance. The proposed framework is applied to a real-world dataset, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the new evaluation method.

We investigate the properties of a Fermi gas with spin greater than or equal to one-half, interacting through a repulsive force. By employing the mean-field Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov theory, we examine the phase transitions in two-dimensional systems and find that the type of transition shifts from Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless to topological for higher spin values. Furthermore, our results indicate that the critical temperature decreases with increasing spin. Additionally, we observe that the topological order parameter exhibits a plateau at low temperatures, and this plateau's value depends on the spin value.

The relationship between pulsars and gamma-ray emitting pulsars is examined, focusing on how the rotating energy loss rate affects their position on the empirical gamma-ray 'death line'. It is suggested that the observed 'death line' is a result of the competition between the rotation energy loss rate and the surface temperature of the pulsar. The surface temperature is the primary factor limiting the gamma-ray emission in cool pulsars, whereas the rotation energy loss rate becomes the limiting factor in hot pulsars. The surface temperature is the primary parameter determining the position of pulsars on the 'death line', and the observed correlation between the rotation energy loss rate and surface temperature is a secondary effect. We have developed a new method to study the properties of rotating superfluids in the presence of spin-orbit coupling. This method is based on a modified Landau-de Gennes theory that takes into account the effects of magnetorotons. Our results show that the magnetorotons in the specific quantum states of $^6$Li-23 exhibit unique properties that depend on their orientation. Specifically, the magnetorotons in the two states have opposite effects on their surroundings. This distinction is crucial for understanding how these states transition into each other as the rotation speed increases. Our findings also suggest that certain experimental measurements, such as the magnetization of the condensate, can be used to distinguish between these two states.

The Italian Telescope EEO Network, a part of the INAF Astronomical Observatory, is a country-wide system comprising 15 telescopes and 9 associated units located across Italy. This network, which is designed to enhance the nation's astronomical capabilities, is built around INAF's headquarters in Rome and is intended for both research and public outreach. This comprehensive system, which is accessible to the general public, is unique in its structure and scope. This document outlines the network's key features, objectives, and functionalities.

This paper explores the behavior of the solution to the spatially homogeneous, fully linearized Boltzmann equation, under the assumption of a cutoff by a given function $\zeta$. The study focuses on the effect of the parameter $\gamma$ on the solution's behavior, particularly in the context of the Grand Lebesgue Space. The findings indicate that the solution is the uniform limit of a family of solutions to the Boltzmann equation, with $\gamma$ taking on specific values, thereby providing a partial solution to an open problem posed by Snire.

This study investigates the performance of machine learning models trained on data contaminated with noise and generalizes their behavior to unseen scenarios. A classification task is defined using a synthetic dataset, and its underlying rules are revealed. Performance metrics are measured in both controlled and unpredictable environments. Models trained on noisy data exhibit better performance on noisy data but surprisingly worse on clean data compared to those trained on clean data alone. A theoretical analysis is presented, suggesting that models trained on noisy data can still be effective in some cases, albeit with the observed performance discrepancy.

This paper investigates the classification of linear isometries between distinct types of cyclic orbit codes, specifically those generated by $N$ and $N+1$, where $N$ is a positive integer. The study focuses on the properties of isometries between constant-weight codes, including those between Reed-Muller codes and the individual MacWilliams identities associated with these codes. The work also involves the classification of isometries between BMAC and RMAC codes, as well as the classification of isometries between BMAC and BMAC-like codes.

The binary star WOCS 11028 consists of a white dwarf and a companion, which is likely a white dwarf, but the exact nature of the companion is uncertain. The companion is either a white dwarf or a helium shell burning star. The binary system's properties were determined using light curves from the Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based observations, which were modeled using MESA and matched with evolutionary tracks. The system's age is approximately 4.0 billion years, and its components are approximately 0.55 solar masses and 0.15 solar masses in mass, respectively. The brighter component is currently at the turnoff point of the M67 cluster, while the companion is at a stage where it is burning helium in its core. The system's properties are consistent with the predicted properties of post common envelope binaries, which suggests that the companion may have lost its envelope through the Eddington luminosity limit constraint.

We examine the spectrum of the Jacobi operator with a complex parameter 'c' based on a specific condition involving its argument 'θ'. When 'θ' satisfies a certain range of values, the system of eigenfunctions is complete. Conversely, if 'θ' falls outside this range, the corresponding operator lacks completeness. Furthermore, the set of resonances within this range corresponds to the Jacobi operator's exceptional spectrum.

A recent study by Kang et al. introduced a new volume element method to improve the accuracy of gradient estimation in smoothed particle hydrodynamics, which we have since generalized to include vector field gradients and scalar field gradients. Our findings indicate that the original Kang et al. method excels at estimating scalar field gradients but falls short for vector field gradients. Moreover, we have successfully integrated this enhanced method into a general-purpose smoothed particle hydrodynamics code capable of simulating both solid and fluid flows.

This paper introduces a novel deep learning approach that maps RGB images to hyperspectral images. The proposed method, called PA-DFM, leverages pixel-wise features and their interdependencies to enhance mapping performance. It consists of two key components: a deep function mixture network that combines multiple mappings and a pixel-aware loss network that incorporates hyperspectral prior information. Experimental results on three datasets reveal that PA-DFM outperforms existing methods, with notable improvements in both overall and class-specific performance.

This study introduces a new approach to enhance the precision of street object geolocation through the integration of contextual geographic information. The proposed framework leverages the strengths of both convolutional and recurrent neural networks to analyze the surrounding context of street objects. The incorporation of contextual information significantly boosts the performance of geolocation prediction models. The proposed method is evaluated using a custom dataset of street signs in Beijing, China, where accurate geolocation is crucial for intelligent transportation systems. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms traditional methods, such as the k-Nearest Neighbors approach, by a margin of 2.2 meters in terms of mean squared error.

This study introduces a novel approach to dam reservoir classification using remote sensing data, incorporating metric learning to enhance dam feature representation. The proposed method leverages a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to extract features from dam images, and a Support Vector Machine (SVM) is utilized to classify reservoirs based on the remote features. The incorporation of metric learning is shown to significantly improve the model's performance. The proposed method was tested on a dataset compiled by the World Bank, and its performance was evaluated using the f1-score metric. The results indicate that the proposed method surpasses the baseline model, and its effectiveness was further demonstrated by applying it to the Google Earth dataset.

This research explores the concept of continuous retracts in the context of QFS-spaces, building on a previous finding that continuous images of QFS-spaces are also QFS. The study demonstrates that the retract property can be preserved in certain situations involving continuous maps, but not in all cases. Additionally, it is shown that the relationship between retracts and continuous images holds true within a specific subset of QFS spaces known as compactly definable ones.

This research presents a novel multimodal approach to predicting points of interest, utilizing a combination of visual and textual modalities. We introduce a dual-encoder architecture that can seamlessly integrate multiple modalities, accompanied by a novel loss function for handling unbalanced multimodal data sets. The proposed method was evaluated on the large-scale Google POIM dataset, achieving a record-breaking macro F1 score of 47.21%.

This study examines the relationship between earnings call conversations and stock price fluctuations. By analyzing 10K earnings call transcripts from 2008 to 2014, the research finds that the semantics of these discussions can predict stock movements more effectively than other financial metrics like MACD and Bollinger Bands. Specifically, the call topics of revenue, economic conditions, guidance, and competition are found to be more informative than traditional technical indicators.

This paper investigates the performance of a wireless sensor network that employs a binary quantization method to reduce communication. Each sensor node transmits binary data to the fusion center, which then estimates the mean of the signals. However, due to their limited transmission range, sensors within close proximity to the center can communicate effectively, whereas those farther away must rely on an estimator. To assess the impact of this limited communication range, we introduce a metric called the critical distance, which affects the overall sensing capability of the network. Our findings indicate that the critical distance has a significant influence on the performance of the wireless sensor network.

We've developed a new quantum algorithm for finding a basis of the null space in a given matrix, which is a fundamental problem in linear algebra. Our algorithm builds on the classic Gauss-Jordan elimination method, but incorporates a new approach using the quantum Fourier transform to reduce the number of operations required. By leveraging this approach, we've shown that our algorithm can be more efficient than classical algorithms, especially when dealing with sparse matrices. In fact, our algorithm can solve this problem in a time complexity that's proportional to the square root of the matrix's sparsity, which is a significant improvement over the best classical algorithms. Our findings also suggest that this algorithm can be more efficient than ever before, even for matrices with a constant number of rows.

This study examines compacton solutions within a nonlinear medium described by the KdV equation. We investigate the impact of nonlinearity parameters on compacton shape, amplitude, and speed using a spectral method-based numerical approach. Our findings indicate that the medium's nonlinearity significantly influences compacton shape, causing them to appear more or less pronounced, depending on parameter values. We discovered that compacton profiles can resemble either the classical KdV solitons or more extreme forms, such as higher-order solitons. Additionally, we analyzed how compacton speed and amplitude relate to various nonlinearity parameter combinations and found that the medium's nonlinearity can lead to increased amplitudes and speeds, even surpassing KdV soliton amplitudes and speeds.

The Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) is a versatile framework for investigating novel interactions between standard model particles, and its applications extend to various energy domains, encompassing hadronic, leptonic, and other systems. This text provides an overview of SMEFT and its current experimental implications, with a focus on the potential of future electron-positron colliders to uncover new interactions. The discussion also touches on the potential of SMEFT to inform future research at the ILC and CLIC, and offers a comparison with alternative theories that could explain the observed anomalies in particle physics.

A highly sensitive rotation sensor based on a single, specially designed atom circuit offers precise measurements. The sensor's design, featuring a coherent atom circuit with multiple energy states, enables it to detect a wide range of rotations. The sensor's performance is improved by using a non-optical method to reduce its sensitivity to temperature changes, which is particularly beneficial for its operation. The sensor's capabilities are further analyzed in the context of a navigation system.

The rapid accumulation of data from high-throughput experiments has made it possible to develop comprehensive models of entire living cells. These models have the potential to revolutionize our understanding of biological systems and their applications in medicine. However, the current lack of standardized models and tools hinders their widespread adoption. To address this issue, we propose a new framework for creating whole-cell models based on a unified format for experimental data and simulations. This framework, which is open-source and modular, enables researchers to work together and share their models. We also provide a web-based platform for sharing and visualizing whole-cell models, and we invite the scientific community to contribute their models and help shape the future of whole-cell modeling.

Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved object image search capabilities, but current systems are limited to using a single view image. This restricts their performance in real-world scenarios where images can be captured from various angles. To address this issue, we present a novel approach that enables object image search using multi-view images. Our proposed method involves two key components: a query and database re-ranking module, which leverages the benefits of multiple views, and a module that generates synthetic views to enhance the search results. Comprehensive experiments on the Caltech-256 dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study introduces a novel two-stage machine learning approach for identifying and classifying epileptic seizures from EEG data. The first stage employs a multi-centroid strategy to determine the presence of seizures, and the second stage utilizes a multi-pass method to identify the onset and termination times of seizures. A comparison of the proposed approach with traditional algorithms revealed that it outperforms HMM, SVM, and ANN methods. Furthermore, this approach was found to be superior to the conventional two-stage algorithm (SVM-Sec) in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, and also exhibited improved results in terms of F-score, Matthew's correlation coefficient, and Kappa coefficient.

We have developed a method to locate dark siren sources using gravitational wave (GW) observations, which relies on the correlation between the GW amplitude and the redshift of the source. This approach is independent of the amplitude-redshift relationship derived from electromagnetic observations, allowing for the estimation of the Hubble constant without prior knowledge of the GW amplitude scale. By applying this method to the GW source population, we can constrain the Hubble constant with a precision of 10% or better. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the use of dark siren sources with a redshift distribution similar to that of the GW source population will provide the most accurate Hubble constant measurements.

The QALD-9 dataset, a benchmark for question answering in Knowledge Graphs, has a significant limitation – it only includes questions in English, making it difficult for systems to handle multilingual settings. To address this issue, we have expanded the dataset, created QALD-9-plus, by adding multilingual questions in Dutch, Spanish, and German, as well as incorporating new datasets from the OpenQA repository. This will enable us to assess the performance of Knowledge Graph Question Answering systems in a multilingual environment. We have also conducted experiments with the QALD-9-plus dataset, comparing different systems and question types, and found that the additional data sets improve the systems' performance, especially in answering questions with multiple answers.

This paper explores the concept of 'hindsight summarization', a method for summarizing past events to improve future performance. It presents a novel algorithm, 'Hindsight Summary Learning', which uses a neural network to create a summary of past experiences and demonstrate that this summary can be used to improve future performance. Our results show that this approach can be used to improve performance by reducing the amount of data needed for training, and can even be used to improve performance on tasks that were not previously experienced.

In medical image analysis, deep learning models are increasingly being used, but they often rely on data that is biased and may not reflect real-world scenarios, leading to concerns about their performance in untested populations. This study investigates the impact of such biases on models that are not specifically designed to combat them, and how they can transfer to new, unrelated datasets. We tested this effect on a diverse set of 15 medical image datasets, and found that biases present in one population can affect the performance of models in another, often in a predictable manner. This knowledge can be used to identify and mitigate biases in existing datasets, ultimately improving the reliability of deep learning models in medical imaging.

This study introduces a new loss function called Smooth Proxy-Anchor Loss, which enhances the performance of Metric Learning methods. It is based on a novel data augmentation technique that involves randomly moving the anchor points within a predefined range. This process is repeated multiple times and the loss is calculated as the average of each iteration. We also propose a method to optimize the augmentation schedule. Our approach is inspired by the concept of Smooth-LQPA, which is designed to minimize the loss function by introducing a new optimization technique. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method by comparing it to other state-of-the-art Metric Learning methods on the MS-COCO and VehicleID datasets.

We have developed a new statistical approach, the mark weighted galaxy number count variance, which can be used to study the relationship between galaxy distribution and cosmological models. This method, which incorporates data from the South Pole Telescope and the Atacama Cosmology Telescope, allows us to analyze the effects of galaxy bias and magnification on our understanding of the universe. Our results show that this new approach provides stronger constraints on certain cosmological parameters than previous methods, and that it is more robust to variations in galaxy bias. We have also found that this new approach provides a more accurate understanding of the mass-observable relation than previous methods, which were based on galaxy density.

We have developed a novel approach to calculate the action of superfluids in the presence of external magnetic fields, based on the concept of gauge invariance. This method is applied to superfluid vortices in a two-dimensional environment and yields a distinct result when compared to the well-known action for superfluid $^4$He. Our findings suggest that the action is analogous to that of superfluid $^3$He$^*$. We have also investigated the behavior of a superfluid when its quasiparticle effective mass varies spatially and found that the action is modified accordingly.

Large-area PhotoMultiplier Devices (MAPDs) are crucial for detecting gamma-rays in space-based experiments. These devices consist of multiple pixels, allowing for the analysis of single-photon signals and noise. In this study, a MAPD with 5x5 pixels was exposed to a narrow gamma-ray beam, analyzing the resulting signals in terms of energy and timing. The device's performance was evaluated using the signal-to-noise ratio and its relationship with the number of pixels involved. The study also investigated the device's ability to distinguish between gamma-rays and cosmic rays, finding that the device's characteristics are well-suited for this purpose. The device's performance was further assessed using a statistical method, which revealed its potential to identify gamma-rays among cosmic rays. The study's findings are significant for the development of space-based gamma-ray experiments.
This paper investigates sectional genera in Gorenstein rings, deriving new results that characterize Gorenstein rings through specific invariants of sectional genera.

The effect of hydrostatic pressure on the structure of multiferroic Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ was examined using high-pressure synchrotron x-ray diffraction. The results showed that as pressure increased, the unit cell parameters expanded, leading to a phase transition at 2.5 GPa. The phase transition was characterized by a significant increase in the unit cell parameters along the a axis, while the unit cell parameters along the b and c axes expanded at a slower rate. The phase transition was found to be reversible, allowing for the creation of high-pressure conditions up to 4.5 GPa. The application of high pressure led to a significant increase in the magnetoelectric coefficient, reaching a value of 1.5 mV, while the spontaneous magnetization remained relatively stable. The results suggest that high-pressure conditions can significantly enhance the multiferroic properties of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$.

The field of transaction cost analysis (TCA) is rapidly evolving, driven by the increasing availability of big data and sophisticated algorithmic trading systems. As a result, brokers are now able to offer more precise and reliable execution services, which necessitates the development of advanced algorithms that can effectively optimize orders and minimize costs. However, the numerous broker-specific algorithms in use today hinder the ability to accurately compare their performance, particularly when considering the inherent uncertainties associated with execution slippage. This paper proposes a novel Bayesian framework for TCA that utilizes Monte Carlo simulations to address these challenges and enable brokers to compare their algorithms more effectively. By leveraging this framework, the study also examines the impact of various market conditions on the relative effectiveness of different broker algorithms.

A compact, widely adaptable add-drop filter has been created within the L and C bands, spanning a 20 GHz range.  The device was developed using a single silicon nanowire and a side coupled waveguide, allowing for the creation of a shared optical port.  The side coupled waveguide acts as a movable optical component, enabling the creation of a moving optical channel.  The moving optical channel is then connected to the main nanowire through a fixed optical component, creating the desired add-drop functionality.  The moving optical component is created using a silicon nitride membrane and can be precisely positioned using a piezoelectric actuator.  The device was optimized to achieve a high Q factor, resulting in a measured transmission of up to 0.9 within the desired bandwidth.  The device was also able to achieve a high isolation of up to 20 dB within the same bandwidth.  The device was also able to achieve a high level of wavelength accuracy, with a measured wavelength accuracy of less than 0.1% across a 20 GHz range. The spread of COVID-19 has been a global concern, with the disease spreading rapidly across the world.  Despite the efforts of many countries to implement vaccination campaigns, the effectiveness of these campaigns is still not well understood.  This study uses machine learning techniques to analyze online data from social media platforms, such as Twitter, to model the progression of the disease.  By comparing these models to more traditional approaches that rely on data from official sources, such as death records, our research highlights the value of non-traditional data in improving our understanding of the pandemic's evolution.  Furthermore, our research demonstrates that these models can be used to forecast future trends in the pandemic, enabling more effective public health interventions.

To improve image compression, we need a more efficient statistical model of images. Our novel PILC framework uses a hierarchical latent variable model to represent images as layers of increasingly abstract features, enabling the compression of complex details without sacrificing visual quality. By separating features into independent blocks, PILC can compress images more effectively than existing methods like PNG, achieving a 27% improvement. Additionally, PILC can compress images at a lower bitrate than HEVC while maintaining superior visual quality, outperforming it by 33%.

Using data collected by the LHCb experiment from high-energy proton collisions in 2016, researchers have conducted a thorough search for the rare $B^{+} \to D_s^{+} \eta \pi^{+}$ decay. This investigation utilized a dataset of 475 pb$^{-1}$ and found no instances of the $D_s^{+} \eta$ final state. As a result, an upper bound of 5.1 x 10$^{-8}$ was established at 95% confidence level for the $B^{+} \to D_s^{+} \eta$ $\pi^{+}$ branching fraction, representing the most precise measurement to date.

Optimal transport theory has gained significant attention in machine learning and statistics due to its mathematical framework and numerous applications. However, the current OT distances are highly susceptible to outliers, which makes them less reliable. To address this issue, we propose a novel distance metric, which is based on optimal transport between measures with pre-identified outliers. This modified distance is more robust and can be computed efficiently using existing optimization techniques. We also explore the concept of outlier transport, which is a divergence measure that can be used to segment data with outliers. By incorporating outlier detection, this approach can lead to more accurate results compared to traditional outlier removal methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods through numerical experiments on various applications, including anomaly detection, anomaly segmentation, and robust clustering.

To enhance human-machine collaboration, researchers need to develop artificial intelligence that can adapt to humans, be easy to interact with, and learn from interactions. However, current approaches are limited by the lack of human-annotated data and the difficulty of designing algorithms that can effectively collaborate with humans. In this study, we propose a new approach to improve AI performance in human-machine collaboration by leveraging human-centric strategies. We developed a reinforcement learning framework that allows agents to learn from interactions with humans and to prioritize human preferences over efficiency. Our experiments on a robot-guided navigation task demonstrated that incorporating human-centric learning strategies can significantly improve performance and lead to more efficient and effective human-robot collaboration.

The generation splitting spectrum in Gensplit theory is examined in detail, focusing on its effects on proton decay. This analysis is crucial for designing future experiments. A key finding is that the observed masses of the 1/2+ baryon states in Gensplit theory can be accurately reproduced only if the first and second generations have significantly different masses. This generation splitting spectrum is then applied to explain the recently discovered pentaquark states.

The effectiveness of visualizations in facilitating insights and decision-making is influenced by their ability to convey information effectively.  Research has shown that certain types of visualizations, such as bar charts and scatter plots, can be used to answer a variety of analytical and comparative questions.  However, the relationship between the type of question being asked and the type of visualization used is not well understood.  This study examines the relationship between the type of question being asked and the type of visualization used, with a focus on the ability of pie charts to answer comparative and non-comparative questions.  The study found that individuals are able to use pie charts to answer both comparative and non-comparative questions, but that they are more effective at answering non-comparative questions.  The study also found that individuals who are familiar with pie charts are able to use them more effectively than those who are not, regardless of their domain expertise.  The study's findings suggest that the type of question being asked and the individual's level of experience with the visualization are important factors in determining the effectiveness of visualizations.

We investigate the computational properties of the open induction principle in the context of formal axiomatization. Our analysis reveals a connection between the open induction operator and the concept of clause set cycles. By establishing a criterion for identifying these cycles, we are able to demonstrate that the application of the open induction principle a finite number of times can be effectively determined. Additionally, we show that the set of all possible open inductions forms an infinite sequence that does not terminate.

This paper presents a modified version of the Shortest Path Kernel that enables the efficient comparison of large graphs by breaking it down into the comparison of smaller graph segments, or "segments". This allows for the computation of the kernel's value without the need for exponential time, making it more feasible for the analysis of large graphs. The proposed approach is demonstrated through its application to the task of graph matching and retrieval, where it outperforms the original Shortest Path Kernel in terms of computational efficiency.

A novel approach to training machine learning models for simulating molecular dynamics has been developed, utilizing a combination of supervised learning and knowledge distillation techniques. The method involves training a model to replicate the time-evolution of molecular systems by learning from the output of a more computationally intensive classical potential. The approach involves two training mechanisms: the first involves directly learning the time-evolution of molecular systems from reference data, and the second involves learning to mimic the underlying potential energy surface. By combining these mechanisms, the model can be effectively trained to reproduce both the short-term and long-term dynamics of molecular systems. The method was tested on a range of small molecules and a protein, and was found to be effective in reproducing the time-evolution of molecular systems. The results showed that the model can be trained to produce high-fidelity dynamics, and can be used to simulate molecular systems with reduced computational cost.

In this study, we develop a model for resolving the electricity distribution issue using concepts from cooperative game theory and fair division. Our approach involves transforming the electricity distribution challenge into a cake-cutting problem, where a neutral agent allocates a total amount of electricity fairly among consumers. We investigate the computational complexity of determining a fair division of electricity and explore the feasibility of finding a fair and efficient allocation. Additionally, we investigate the computational complexity of determining the core of the electricity distribution game and identify scenarios in which it can be calculated efficiently.

This study introduces a new method to enhance the accuracy of event information collection through coreference resolution of event pairs in news articles. We developed a coreference resolution system that resolves both event mention pairs and event coreference in two separate processes, using a bidirectional long short-term memory (BLSTM) network to model the coreference resolution of event mentions and event coresference. We also designed a new feature to model the coreference relationship between event pairs. Experimental results on the ACE2004 and ACE2008 datasets show that our approach outperforms existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance in event coreference resolution.

We explore the potential of mixed-integer programming for the complementarity knapsack problem by developing novel cutting-plane methods that can identify new, valid inequalities that define facets for the problem. Additionally, we examine the relationship between these new inequalities and existing ones, as well as their impact on mixed-integer programming solvers. Our research yields the discovery of 15 distinct valid inequalities that define facets for the problem, and we demonstrate that they outperform other state-of-the-art cutting-plane methods. Moreover, we identify a connection between these new inequalities and a specific type of inequalities that define the problem, and we establish that they can be derived from a geometric property of the problem. Our results also reveal that these new inequalities can significantly improve the performance of mixed-integer programming solvers, and we demonstrate that they can be integrated with other cutting-plane methods to enhance their effectiveness.
This paper introduces the concept of a torsion restriction, enabling the establishment of connections between generalized (m,n)-Jordan centralizers and torsion restrictions.

We investigate the role of Wigner constraints within the context of the Weinberg soft factor computation. Our analysis reveals that these constraints are indispensable for solving the Weinberg factor and also plays a crucial part in evaluating observables via multi-time correlators. Furthermore, we provide a detailed explanation for the necessity of Winger constraints and derive the Weinberg operator from the Ward identities.

We examine the separation condition for orthogonal projections onto the images of a family of nonlinear projection-type operators, and establish connections between this condition and transversality properties of the projections. In specific cases, such as when the family consists of retracts or has a certain commutativity, we investigate and summarize the condition for transversality.

In imitator tasks, the amount of data required from an expert can be significantly reduced by using a more efficient demonstration approach. However, this study reveals that demonstration efficiency is not just a function of the amount of data needed, but also of how well the demonstrations are adapted to distribution shifts. To quantify this, we define demonstration efficiency as a measure of how well demonstrations can adapt to various types of shifts, including changes in dynamics, observations, and reward functions. We then show that demonstration efficiency is related to imitation learning performance and that it can be used to select the most effective demonstrations. Furthermore, we propose a new method for estimating demonstration efficiency and demonstrate its effectiveness in various scenarios.

The intrinsic anomalous Hall effect is typically associated with materials that lack inversion symmetry. However, we have now predicted a previously unknown third-order anomalous Hall effect in centrosymmetric materials that have a specific type of spin-orbit coupling. This effect is unique in that it relies on the interaction between multiple spin-orbit interactions and is not influenced by magnetic fields or other external factors. We have identified a class of materials that may exhibit this phenomenon, including certain heavy-element compounds. Our findings have the potential to expand the scope of materials that can be used to study the anomalous Hall effect and could also lead to the discovery of new materials with enhanced spin-hall conductivity.

We introduce a novel approach for visualizing performance metrics in relation to
application execution contexts, grounded in the principles of association rule
learning. By leveraging hierarchical performance profiles and call graph
analyses, this method identifies connections between performance bottlenecks
and their associated execution contexts. The resulting visualization, an
association rule call graph, showcases the most critical bottlenecks alongside
their respective execution contexts, enabling an in-depth exploration of the
underlying relationships. We demonstrate the utility of this approach in the
context of the SPECjvm2005 application.

The widely used One Billion Word Benchmark (OBMB) has been instrumental in evaluating language models' capabilities, yet it has significant limitations. Specifically, the task's narrow focus on predicting words from preceding contexts, which often lack sufficient information for accurate predictions, makes it an unsuitable benchmark for evaluating language models' full potential. We demonstrate that, in many cases, the OBMB requires models to generate words not based on the preceding context, but rather to compensate for the dataset's insufficiencies. Consequently, the benchmark's results are not a reliable measure of a model's language generation capabilities. In an effort to create a more effective benchmark, we introduce the 1GB Image Benchmark, which assesses a model's ability to generate coherent text given an image as input.

We have conducted a comprehensive study of the X-ray and radio characteristics of a major solar flare that occurred on August 17, 2010, which was triggered by a M5.50 X-ray flare. Our research utilized data from the Reuven Ramaty High Energy Solar Spectroscopic C3 instrument on board the Swift satellite and the Nobeyama Radioheliograph. Our findings reveal that the radio brightness temperature in the source exhibited a complex behavior, initially increasing and then decreasing in response to the X-ray flare, which is consistent with previous observations of solar flares. Our analysis also shows that the radio brightness temperature in the source varied in a non-linear fashion, with the highest value occurring at a specific energy range. Furthermore, we observed a significant delay between the X-ray and radio emissions, which is consistent with previous studies. Our research suggests that the radio emission is generated by electron bremsstrahlung in a hot, dense plasma, which is supported by the observed radio brightness temperature and the plasma's high density. Our findings also indicate that the radio emission is not a single, isolated event, but rather a recurring phenomenon that is linked to the X-ray flare.

Convolutional processes are increasingly being used in image analysis, and the resulting feature maps can be analyzed to identify patterns and anomalies. This paper proposes a statistical framework for detecting anomalies in image data, where the feature maps are treated as independent observations under a spatial Markov model. The method involves estimating the local mean and variance of the feature maps, and the results indicate that the proposed approach outperforms existing techniques in terms of accuracy and speed. The approach has been successfully applied to various real-world scenarios, including image classification, segmentation, and super-resolution, and the results show promising performance in these tasks.

This research focuses on the theoretical analysis of solutions for the $p$-dispersive Kadomtsev–Petviashvili I equation with a p value less than 2, specifically its inhomogeneous version. We demonstrate that under certain conditions, the solution to this equation can be represented as a series expansion of its inhomogeneous part, with each term generated through a specific iterative process. However, our findings contradict traditional methods, as we show that small levels of dispersion can lead to divergence in this iterative process. We establish a new approach to solving the equation and provide a more accurate representation of its solutions.

In open quantum systems, Kramers' degeneracy breaks down due to loss of symmetry, 
but surprisingly, this breakdown is not directly linked to thermal equilibrium. 
However, a breakdown of Kramers' degeneracy does occur in a system's relaxation 
state, which is a nonequilibrium steady state. This nonequilibrium state is 
characterized by the simultaneous violation and subsequent revival of Kramers' 
degeneracy, resulting in a double-peaked energy distribution. This phenomenon 
is attributed to the nonequilibrium nature of the steady state and is not seen 
in equilibrium conditions. This phenomenon is observed in a simple model system 
with a lossy double-well potential and is also influenced by the introduction 
of a two-level system. This model system can be experimentally realized using 
superconducting qubits.

This paper introduces a novel 3-D neural network-based channel estimation technique for wireless OFDM systems. By utilizing a 3-D convolutional neural network to predict channel state information from received signal data, the proposed method eliminates the need for complex channel modeling. Experimental results indicate that the 3-D CNN based approach achieves a 100% accuracy in CSI prediction for various scenarios, including those with changing environments and moving transmitters, significantly outperforming traditional channel estimation methods.

This study examines the application of the Gini, Atkinson, and Theil indexes in assessing income inequality within the framework of a two-factor production function. We consider a variety of technological relationships, including both fixed costs and decreasing returns, to better understand how these measures are affected. Our analysis reveals that the Gini coefficient, Atkinson index, and Theil indexes are sensitive to different aspects of income distribution. We find that the Gini and Theil indexes are influenced by the degree of concavity of returns to scale, while the Gini and Atkinson indexes are affected by the level of income. Our results show that fixed costs can increase income inequality, according to the Theil index, but have no impact on the Gini coefficient or Atkinson index.

We examine the tempered spectral projection kernel $P_{\chi, \lambda}(z,w)$ which expresses the sum of Laplace eigenfunctions at a compact manifold $M$ weighted by a smooth character $\chi$ and decay parameter $\lambda$. This study focuses on the large-$\lambda$ behavior of $P_{\chi, \lambda}(z,w)$ and its implications for the trace, showing that it follows a specific probability distribution under certain conditions. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the distribution with a random walk on a compact manifold with polynomial speed-cutoff conditions and its asymptotic behavior.

This paper introduces MARINLINGA, a novel algorithm that generates the original graph from its line graph. Unlike other algorithms, MARINLINGA doesn't require the original graph's size, maximum degree, or maximum clique size as inputs. It's straightforward to implement and can serve as a foundation for future line graph based indexing techniques. MARINLINGA's performance is demonstrated through experiments on both artificial and real-world datasets.

Lee-Lee's 2017 conjecture for the punctured disc group G, involving elements with infinite order, suggests that any element with infinite order in G is either a "real" or "imaginary" root of a polynomial. This conjecture has significant implications for the classification of elements with infinite order in G, and its validity has been demonstrated for specific cases, notably those with finite order multiples. This study confirms Lee-Lee's conjecture for the class of elements with finite order multiples in G, and its consequences are examined, including the recovery of certain results previously established by other methods.

In software development, the practice of preserving unnecessary code elements, or bloat, is a widespread issue. This study investigates the persistence of such bloat over time in the influential open-source projects, Eclipse and Apache, by examining the relationship between code modules. Our analysis reveals that a significant portion of direct dependencies remain redundant in subsequent versions, with a notable $50.4-52.5\%$ of these dependencies still being bloated in the next major release. Moreover, the bloat level in transitive dependencies is even more pronounced, with only $7.4-9.2\%$ of these indirect relationships being reduced in the next version. Notably, the bloat in these indirect relationships is more resistant to reduction than direct relationships, with a $40\%$ decrease rate, compared to a $20\%$ decrease rate for direct relationships.

The concept of one-way control is typically associated with quantum mechanics, yet it has also been successfully applied in classical systems, particularly within the realm of polymer science. This research explores the theoretical and experimental aspects of one-way control in systems of entangled bi-photons, with a focus on how the spatial arrangement of polymer molecules is manipulated. Our findings indicate that the required polymer density is significantly lower than in classical implementations, with experiments able to replicate the process using a setup featuring two single-layer waveguides with a 3D photonic crystal.

This research introduces a method for pinpointing pivotal moments and identifying the worst-case data sets that challenge the robustness of multistage distributionally robust optimization solutions. By analyzing the behavior of a perturbation measure under data uncertainty, the approach identifies critical scenarios that render the measure ineffective. These critical scenarios are then used to craft worst-case data sets that exploit the measure. We demonstrate the method's application in the context of multistage stochastic programming and show its efficacy through a numerical study.

In this research, we present a novel approach to action anticipation that leverages the capabilities of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in conjunction with Radial Basis Function (RBP) kernels. Our hypothesis is that GNNs possess inherent advantages in anticipating actions, and their performance can be further optimized through the incorporation of RBP kernels. To validate this assertion, we developed a GNN model that incorporates RBP kernels and demonstrated its superior performance in anticipating actions compared to existing state-of-the-art models. Our results indicate that the proposed model achieves a significant improvement in anticipation accuracy, with a notable gain of 5% in average precision on the 50-Sentences dataset. Furthermore, we conducted an ablation study to assess the effectiveness of RBP kernels and their associated parameters, and our findings suggest that the proposed model is more robust and efficient than traditional GNNs.

We investigate the behavior of observables in a system undergoing thermalization and deep thermalization processes.  By comparing the outcomes of these processes, we identify key differences.  Specifically, we observe that regular thermalization yields a power-law correction to thermalized results, whereas deep thermalization results in exponential corrections.  These corrections can be understood through the lens of the Hawking unitarity and the AdS/CFT correspondence, respectively.  Additionally, we explore the implications of these processes on the formation of black holes and the information paradox.

This research explores the relationship between nuclear operators on spaces of tempered ultradifferentiable functions and those of Sobolev type, also investigating their connection to pseudo-differential operators that operate on these spaces.

This study examines the impact of the Line-of-Sight (LOS) condition on 5G base station deployments and the surrounding electromagnetic environment. We have developed a predictive model to estimate the exposure levels resulting from 5G exposure configurations, taking into account the LOS condition. Our analysis reveals that the LOS condition significantly affects exposure levels, with exposure reductions ranging from 50% to 80% in comparison to LOS scenarios.

Deep learning models have been found to perform poorly on out-of-distribution data, often misclassifying it. To address this issue, we propose using CODEs - a type of perturbation that alters the input data in a way that highlights its differences. We demonstrate that applying CODEs to input data significantly improves the performance of both OOD detection and classification tasks. We also show that a simple classifier can be trained to identify these CODEs and effectively distinguish between in-distribution and out-of-distribution data. Furthermore, we suggest a new method for estimating the reliability of a model's confidence by measuring the proportion of CODEs that trigger it to reject OOD data. Our research provides a new approach to OOD detection and offers a range of innovative applications for improving the reliability of deep learning models.

Theoretical predictions for jet distributions at the Large Hadron Collider are significantly improved by next-to-leading-order calculations, which incorporate the effects of multiple radiation processes. In particular, the leading-color approximation allows for the efficient calculation of jet cross sections up to a certain level of precision. To further refine these predictions, the complete color-spectrum calculation is applied to the virtual terms, with the residual color-sunglasses effect approximated using a specific method. This approach is demonstrated with precise predictions for the hadron-level jet transverse momentum spectrum in $pp$ collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, achieved through a numerical integration technique.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have led to significant advancements in visual recognition tasks. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of these models largely relies on the quality of the training data, which is often limited and biased. To address this issue, we propose an innovative approach to enhance model generalization by utilizing unlabeled data. Our method, which we call Self-Training with Co-Optimization, involves a two-stage training process. Initially, we employ a model trained on a limited labeled dataset. Subsequently, we utilize the initial model to generate pseudo-labels for the remaining data, which we then use to fine-tune the model in a self-supervised manner. Crucially, we optimize the initial model and the pseudo-labels simultaneously to maximize their mutual dependency. Through extensive experiments on various visual recognition tasks, we demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing state-of-the-art methods.

In the realm of outlier detection, handling the influence of correlated input attributes is a significant challenge. To address this, we introduce RECol, a novel approach that enables learning from interdependent input characteristics. RECol achieves this by incorporating a conditional independence test into the outlier detection process, thereby modeling the intricate relationships between the input features. RECol's ability to detect correlations between the input attributes and its capacity to adapt to unknown interdependencies make it a robust method. RECol's effectiveness is demonstrated through its ability to outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in synthetic and real-world datasets.

This research investigates the non-linear evolution equation with a non-local term and a singular logarithmic function, specifically focusing on the impact of initial conditions on the solution's regularity properties. Our study demonstrates that the solution exhibits a loss of regularity, and in certain scenarios, it even becomes unbounded as time progresses. Furthermore, we establish that the solution possesses a specific H\"older continuity property, and we examine its behavior in the context of an initial value problem within a half-space.

A minimal effective model is developed to account for the observed anomalies in the muon's magnetic moment and the $(g-2)_\mu$ value, as well as the small neutrino masses. This model involves operators of varying dimensions, with those of dimension 7 being particularly relevant due to their connection to the GIM mechanism. As a result, the mass of the mediators in these operators is significantly reduced, with their mass being constrained by the combination of $(g-2)_{\mu-2}$ and neutrino mass constraints. Furthermore, the model includes a dimension 5 operator that introduces a new Higgs mass term, with its mass being constrained by the $(g-2)_{\mu-2}$ and neutrino mass constraints. Additionally, the model's parameter space is explored in the context of the small neutrino masses.

The ability of neurons to adjust their connections through short-term plasticity plays a vital role in the brain's functioning, yet the mechanisms behind this are still not fully understood. This study investigates the role of short-term plasticity in the development of complex neural behavior through a mathematical model of a neuron with time-dependent synaptic adjustments. The model's ability to replicate various neural responses was confirmed through numerical simulations, and further analysis revealed that short-term plasticity can give rise to the formation of synchronized neural bursts. This discovery holds significant implications for the brain's functioning, and highlights the importance of short-term plasticity in neural processing.

We've developed a quantum-classical correspondence theory centered on the concept of a flux tube, which is a topological entity that captures the quantized properties of a magnetic field generated by a solenoid. This theory is exemplified by a mathematical model of a planar rotor with a spin of 1/2, which interacts with a magnetic field produced by a solenoid. The model reveals that the rotor's motion can be understood as a spiral path, with its trajectory influenced by the solenoid's radius and the angle of the magnetic field. The model also shows that the rotor's wave function can be represented as a combination of two Gaussian functions, each associated with a specific energy level. The corresponding classical dynamics of the system can be derived from the Schrödinger equation, which provides a connection between the quantum and classical regimes. The model's results are consistent with experimental data obtained from the study of a planar rotor with a spin of 1/2, which was placed in a magnetic field generated by a solenoid.

We investigate the Brownian motion of a particle in a 3-dimensional space with a moving wall that represents a particle's surface. The particle's survival probability is found to depend on the number of collisions with the wall within a logarithmic time frame. The number of these collisions is proportional to the logarithm of time. The survival probability is expressed as a series of exponential decay terms, each corresponding to a specific number of collisions with the wall. The coefficients of these terms are calculated using a method that involves solving a 3-dimensional space boundary problem for the Laplace operator. The resulting solution is a fundamental solution of the Laplace equation with a moving boundary. The particle's survival probability is found to be bounded from below by an exponential decay term with a rate proportional to the logarithm of time. The coefficients of the exponential decay terms are found to be related to the eigenvalues of a Sturm-Liouville operator, which are calculated using a method that involves solving a 2-dimensional space boundary problem for the Helmholtz equation. The resulting solution is a fundamental solution of the Helmholtz equation with a moving boundary. The coefficients of the exponential decay terms are found to be related to the eigenvalues of a 2-dimensional space boundary problem for the Helmholtz equation. The resulting solution is a fundamental solution of the Helmholtz equation with a moving boundary. The coefficients of the exponential decay terms are found to be related to the eigenvalues of a 2-dimensional

We've developed a method to encode the combinatorial properties of Heegaard splittings for integer homology three-spheres that contain hyperbolic L-space knots. This method relies on a representation of formal semigroups with a specific structure, built from the L-space surgery coefficients. We found that any such semigroup can be represented using at most five generators and have at most nine relations. This finding connects the number of generators to the sphere's L-space surgery coefficients and highlights a connection between the semigroup's growth and the number of L-spaces a knot undergoes.
We derive the compressible Euler equations from the Vlasov-Poisson system in the long-collision mean-field limit, applicable to weakly-degenerate hard potentials.

This study presents a novel approach to fusing multiple detectors in real-time, aiming to enhance the performance of individual models and achieve a more stable ensemble. By utilizing a Bayesian framework to model the prediction distributions of different detectors, the proposed method enables the estimation of uncertainty in ensemble predictions. To account for potential biases in each detector, the method incorporates a bias correction term, which is estimated through a meta-learning process. Additionally, the approach introduces a dynamic fusion strategy that adapts to the uncertainty of predictions and the distribution of the data. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in improving the performance of individual models and achieving more robust ensembles.

The use of identifiers in code is a crucial aspect of programming languages, significantly impacting how developers understand and maintain software. Research has shown that the naming patterns used in code can either hinder or aid comprehension. This study examines the relationship between identifier naming patterns and cognitive load experienced by developers. Our investigation involves a controlled experiment where 72 developers were tasked with identifying bugs in code.
