We introduce a novel approach to testing for the presence of a structural break in a regression model without relying on certain conditions such as the break point location or the break type. This approach is capable of handling various types of breaks and their combinations in the regression function. The proposed test is non-parametric and robust, allowing for any continuous function as a data generating process. The test has been shown to have an exact size and is asymptotically efficient under certain conditions. The test's performance is further demonstrated through a Monte Carlo study and an application to real-world data analysis.

This study introduces a novel dataset for Arabic social media sentiment analysis, 
consisting of 3,000 annotated posts from Twitter, divided into 2,000 training and 
100 test sentences per class. Utilizing this dataset, we examine the impact of 
multilingual models on social media content analysis and assess the performance 
of models trained on both Arabic and English data. Our results demonstrate that 
models trained on both languages outperform those trained on a single language, 
with a notable improvement of 0.16 in macro F1 score. Furthermore, we found that 
English-language models can excel in Arabic social media analysis, provided they 
are trained on sufficient data.

Brain disorders, which are often characterized by distinct patterns of brain damage, can be challenging to diagnose and classify.  Although the current diagnostic methods are highly reliable, they often fail to provide a definitive answer.  To address this issue, researchers have been exploring the potential of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to identify specific brain regions affected by different disorders.  However, the complexity of fMRI data has made it difficult to analyze, leading to the development of machine learning techniques that can automatically identify patterns in the data.  In this study, we used a deep learning approach to analyze fMRI data from patients with Alzheimer's disease and healthy individuals, and found that it outperformed other machine learning methods in classifying the data.  Our results suggest that deep learning can be a powerful tool for diagnosing brain disorders, and can potentially be used to improve the accuracy of diagnostic methods.

This paper presents a novel approach to the convergence rate analysis of model predictive control. It demonstrates that the rate of convergence can be directly linked to the rate at which control inputs diminish, which in turn is related to the rate at which energy is dissipated. This method is applicable to both linear and nonlinear systems, and can be used in conjunction with existing MPC analysis techniques. Furthermore, the approach is illustrated through numerical solutions of algebraic Riccati equations and numerical simulations of a simple mechanical system and a realistic 3D quadrotor system.

This study presents a comprehensive approach to address the boundary treatment issue in high-order numerical schemes for hyperbolic conservation laws. The proposed method utilizes a spectral basis to construct a series representation of the flux derivative on the cell boundary, ensuring continuity and first-order accuracy, while the second-order term is approximated by a quadratic function to maintain the desired order of accuracy. This new method is demonstrated to be effective in enhancing stability and accuracy when applied to the wave equation and the one-dimensional Euler equations.

We have developed a novel method for creating a highly efficient silicon photonic crystal back reflector that can absorb a wide range of wavelengths. By using a nanoscale silicon film, this structure can be tailored to suit various applications. Our approach involves a simple and scalable fabrication process that can be used to produce a photonic crystal back reflector with a high absorption rate of over 99.9% across a wide spectrum of wavelengths. Our results show that the optical absorption rate can be improved by increasing the thickness of the silicon film, as well as by adjusting the size of the photonic crystal and the depth of the grating. Our findings indicate that this technology has the potential to be used in a wide range of applications, including the development of ultra-efficient silicon lasers and light-emitting diodes.

This paper presents an innovative approach to credal sets through the lens of algebraic structures. We define the algebraic structure known as valuation algebra and its constituent operations, including conjunction, disjunction, and conditioning. We establish that these operations conform to specific axiomatic rules, which in turn characterizes the algebraic structure of credal sets. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical framework for credal set algorithms and identify a particular class of algorithms known as polynomial algorithms. We also demonstrate that algorithms such as sorting and insertion algorithms fall under this category.

We introduce a novel distance metric, the Wasserstein distance, to address the issue of cold-start recommendations in a user-item tensor. Our proposed model, called Wasserstein Recommendation (WRec), utilizes a neural network to learn the Wasserstein distance between user and item embeddings, thereby capturing their relationships. This approach is grounded in the observation that the Wasserstein distance reflects the cost of mapping one probability distribution to another. In the context of recommendations, this distance represents the minimal cost required to transform a user's preference distribution into an item's preference distribution. Our experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of WRec over existing baseline methods, and we further show that incorporating additional item information, such as ratings, enhances the model's performance.

We investigate the quantum information processing capabilities of the GAD channel, specifically focusing on its Gaussian unitary invariant structure. By analyzing the Gaussian approximation of the deGlopper-Aubrun-Miquel (GAM) channel, we demonstrate that the Gaussian approximation of the deGlopper-Aubrun-Miquel (GAM) channel exhibits a non-Markovian characteristic. Furthermore, we show that the Gaussian approximation of the deGlopper-Aubrun-Miquel (GAM) channel's non-Markovian characteristic is distinct from the eternally non-Markovian nature of the quasi-energy non-Markovian model (ENM) GAD channel.

This paper introduces the Conditional Cross-Attentional Routing (CCRAL) approach to enhance model adaptability when processing sequential data with limited training examples. CCRAL is a flexible framework that can be integrated into various neural network architectures, such as Recurrent Neural Networks and Transformers. The primary goal of CCRAL is to create a model that can effectively process test cases with limited training examples. CCRAL achieves this by analyzing the internal routing of neural networks and adapting it to each test case. A key innovation in CCRAL is the introduction of a conditional routing matrix that enables the network to focus on relevant internal information for each test case. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of CCRAL in improving model interpretability and generalization on unseen test data.

The semantic mapping process in robotics is crucial for various applications, but it poses significant challenges due to the need for precise semantic labeling of 3D LiDAR scans. This requirement is particularly demanding due to the high resolution of LiDAR scans and the need for accurate semantic information. To address this issue, we introduce a novel semantic labeling approach that leverages a deep semantic segmentation network to efficiently process LiDAR scans. This approach is designed to be computationally fast and scalable, making it suitable for real-time applications. We also propose a method to handle LiDAR scan connectivity and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through comprehensive experiments on the SemanticKITTI dataset, which show improved performance compared to state-of-the-art methods in terms of semantic segmentation accuracy and wall-time efficiency.

The Rikudo puzzle is an extension of the Pyramady puzzle with added complexity, requiring the placement of even and odd numbers within a grid. We demonstrate that the Rikudo puzzle can be solved efficiently in polynomial time when odd numbers are initially restricted to the puzzle's perimeter.

This study examines the efficiency of Sinkhorn's algorithm in solving a two-person zero-sum game represented by an optimal transport problem with a cost function that can be expressed as a combination of a convex term and a convex term. The goal is to minimize the maximum dual optimal value under a box constraint on the dual variables. The analysis reveals that the computational complexity of Sinkhorn's algorithm is significantly reduced and becomes comparable to solving a single convex problem, outperforming existing methods that consider the dual problem as a separable optimal transport problem. The improved efficiency of Sinkhorn's algorithm is particularly relevant in machine learning applications, where the computational complexity is reduced from O(n^3) to O(n^2).

For the order m with m being even, we consider the generalized modular equation of order m for the complex modular function $\varphi(u)$ derived from the elliptic curve $E: y^2=x^3-u\cdot x+\delta u^{2m}$. Here, the constant $\delta$ is non-zero and the polynomial $P(\phi(u),\delta)=u^{2m}-\delta\phi(u)^m$ has no roots. We then examine the relationship between the solutions of the generalized modular equation and the polynomial $P(\phi(u),\delta)=0$, discovering a unique $(\alpha,\delta)$ pair. Furthermore, this solution is used to find the rational points on the elliptic curve $E$ over the rational function field $\mathbb{Q}(u)$.

We have conducted a comprehensive study of two galaxy lensing systems, J0818-2613 and J1817+2729, using the Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Camera 3. By analyzing high-resolution images, we have precisely determined the positions and redshifts of the deflecting galaxies, identifying them as elliptical galaxies. For J0818-2613, we have measured the deflectors' redshifts at 0.59 and 0.60, and for J1817+2729, we have measured the deflectors' redshifts at 0.2345 and 0.2365. By applying the lens modeling technique, we have successfully reconstructed the mass distributions of the deflectors, revealing that they are early-type galaxies. Our results show that the mass profiles of the deflectors are consistent with a power-law model, and that the central slopes are relatively flat. We have also found that the mass within the inner 5 kiloparsecs is approximately 10^11 solar masses. Our study highlights the importance of high-resolution imaging in understanding galaxy lensing systems, and demonstrates the effectiveness of the lens modeling technique in determining the mass distributions of deflectors.

This study introduces a novel numerical approach to solve the initial problem associated with a $q$-fractional differential equation. The method is based on the difference method, which is further simplified by utilizing the $q$-fractional integration by parts formula. The resulting numerical scheme is then analyzed for its convergence properties, and an error estimate of $O(h^{2-q}_{\Delta})$ is established. To validate the numerical scheme's accuracy, various test cases are considered.

The study of the phonon Hall effect in dielectric materials has been conducted using a first-principles approach. The phonon Hall conductivity in dielectric materials is influenced by the magnetic field's capacity to introduce a nonreciprocal property to the low-frequency acoustic phonons. The results show that certain dielectric materials exhibit a significant phonon Hall effect. Notably, the materials' ability to display a Hall conductivity depends on their crystal structure. The findings suggest that the phonon Hall effect in bulk dielectrics has the potential to be exploited for the manipulation of acoustic phonons.

A novel wide field imaging technique, referred to as the "nod and shuffle" method, has been developed for the Large Binocular Eyes Telescope to enhance its acquisition and alignment process. This technique, an adaptation of the "nod and decode" method, enables the use of a single acquisition image for alignment purposes, significantly reducing acquisition times by 10-15 times compared to traditional methods. The technique's effectiveness has been successfully demonstrated on the Large Binocular Eyes Telescope, resulting in a root mean square plate scale error of 0.05-0.07 inches per pixel. Furthermore, the method's robustness has been confirmed by its ability to function effectively in the presence of atmospheric distortion and telescope misalignment.

In 2011, Chong, Lim, and Ung did an excellent job in solving a long-standing problem posed by Littlewood in 1953, by finding the tightest upper bound for the four-color theorem. This led to a natural inquiry by Chong and Yu to find the tightest upper bounds for the n-color problem in general. This research aims to explore the matrix variations of these inequalities, which have connections to the Lagrange identity, Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, and Bessel's inequality.

We investigate the thermodynamic properties of a black hole that undergoes a change in its charge by analyzing the averaged null energy condition. Our analysis reveals that the averaged null energy condition remains positive throughout the formation and evaporation process, providing a robust thermodynamic stability guarantee.

We investigate the influence of an irrelevant operator with a conformal dimension of dI = dJ - dK, where dJ and dK are integers with dJ > dK, on the trace anomaly of a four-dimensional conformal field theory. This operator is coupled to two chiral operators of dimensions dJ and dK. We demonstrate that the operator's effect on the trace anomaly is to introduce a term proportional to (∇2)ddK-1, where the constant factor depends on the difference dJ - dK. This discovery is relevant to the study of the QCD trace anomaly.

This paper presents a novel method for evaluating the advancement of testbeds in Industrial Control Systems, which are vital for the security of Industrial Internet of Things systems. By employing a real-time assessment of testbed maturity, researchers can create a comprehensive and up-to-date understanding of the global research landscape. This information enables targeted research initiatives that build upon existing projects, ultimately contributing to the development of a cohesive and effective cyber-security framework for IIoT applications.

This study introduces a novel architecture called the greedy-based value representation (GVR), designed to enhance the efficiency of multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms. GVR incorporates a greedy mechanism into the value function, enabling it to represent policies with high returns. By doing so, it can significantly improve the performance of policies learned from data. To validate the effectiveness of GVR, we conducted a series of experiments in multi-agent scenarios, including the classic gridworld setting and the challenging StarCraft II MAPS1_1 map. The results show that GVR can accelerate the training of policies and yield better outcomes.

We introduce StereoSet, a comprehensive dataset of 1,500 stereotypical statements across 4 categories (appearance, behavior, intelligence, and culture) annotated with 5 distinct ratings (neutral to strongly stereotypical) by 3 independent teams of crowdworkers. Our study utilizes this dataset to assess the effectiveness of current language models in recognizing and mitigating stereotypical biases. We also propose a novel method for bias reduction, iterative listwise ranking, which leverages the ratings from StereoSet to fine-tune bias mitigation techniques. Our findings indicate that language models consistently generate stereotypical content and that current debiasing techniques are insufficient, particularly when applied to smaller datasets. We demonstrate that our proposed method, which employs multiple iterations of debiasing and ranking, successfully reduces biases in a dataset-specific manner.

This study introduces a novel approach to optimizing network updates by combining Contextual Multi-Armed-Bandit (CMAB) theory with reinforcement learning. The method involves utilizing real-time network conditions to determine the most effective tilt update strategy. A novel policy, the Tilt Update Policy, is derived from the contextual bandit framework. The tilt update policy is then optimized using reinforcement learning, which is further improved by a proposed federated learning approach. The proposed method is evaluated through extensive simulations, demonstrating its superior performance over conventional methods.

The LHCb experiment has made precise measurements of the CKM angle gamma using the decay process where a B meson decays into a charmed meson, a muon, and a positive or negative electron. These measurements have been conducted in two different mass ranges for the charmed meson, one between 2000-3000 MeV and another above 3000 MeV. The experiment has also been repeated using the conjugate process where the roles of muons and electrons are reversed. The results of these processes are combined to provide a more precise value of gamma, which is found to be -0.046 degrees with a confidence interval of 0.037 degrees. The experiment has also been used to calculate the Br(S)-12 decay rate, which is found to be (4.32 +/- 0.18 +/- 0.07) x 10^-7.

A key advantage of complex symmetry in the context of convex geometry lies in its ability to describe and analyze complex shapes using simpler cross-sections and projections. This property makes complex symmetry an effective tool for understanding complex geometric forms. This brief note serves as a comprehensive introduction to complex symmetry and the intricate relationships between different geometric properties of convex shapes.

The concept of trading personal data has been widely explored in the fields of economics and computer science, with a focus on understanding market behavior and the value of data. However, despite these efforts, there is a significant gap in knowledge regarding how individuals perceive the trade of personal data. Our research involved conducting in-depth interviews with 20 individuals, who were asked to share their thoughts on buying and selling personal data. The participants' responses often deviated from existing market theories, and their perspectives were more complex and nuanced. We identified several key themes that emerged from these interviews, which highlight the need for a more comprehensive framework for understanding the trade of personal data.

This study introduces a novel approach to FTN signaling using deep learning, aiming to decrease the detection complexity by limiting it to a subset of FTN samples. The proposed method involves a neural network that predicts the most valuable FTN samples for transmission, based on the desired balance between detection accuracy and complexity. The approach is flexible, allowing for the selection of samples either before or after detection, and can be easily integrated with existing FTN detection systems without requiring additional training. Simulation results demonstrate that this method can achieve comparable BER performance to existing FTN detection methods, while significantly reducing the detection complexity.

We demonstrate that in certain effect algebras, specifically those being complete atomic distributive lattices, the Frink and order topologies are equivalent under specific conditions, namely when the algebra's order is compatible with its meet and join operations. This result is then applied to show that in such effect algebras, every filter can be expressed as the intersection of upper and lower sets within their order topology, and ultimately establish the topological characteristics of a type of convergence in these filters.

This study introduces SaliencyMix, a straightforward technique that enhances the predictive capabilities of object detection models by combining salient and background information. By incorporating a portion of salient data into the training process, SaliencyMix improves the detection of challenging objects, particularly those with limited training data. We tested SaliencyMix on a range of datasets, including the COCO, VOC, and ADE20K benchmarks, as well as a custom dataset, and found that it consistently boosts model performance. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that SaliencyMix is particularly effective for models struggling with underrepresented object categories.

In 1988, Vershik and Kerov completed a 1985 classification problem initiated by the Lusztig for indecomposable positive traces on infinite-dimensional Iwahori-Hecke algebras. This paper provides a new classification of these traces, offering a distinct and independent classification that differs from Vershik and Kerov's classification.

We investigate how the alignment parameter of galaxies, a measure of their intrinsic shapes, is affected by the gravitational influence of massive clusters. Our analysis utilizes a sample of 1,300 clusters from the Planck catalogue and matches it with a sample of 1,300 clusters from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. We find that the alignment parameter of galaxies, a measure of how the shapes of galaxies are influenced by clusters, is significantly correlated with the mass of clusters. This correlation is observed in both the inner and outer regions of clusters, and it is consistent with the predictions of general relativity. Our results also indicate that the shapes of galaxies are more strongly influenced by clusters in the direction of the cluster's central region. This finding is consistent with the predictions of general relativity. Our analysis further reveals that the alignment parameter of galaxies is more strongly correlated with the shapes of clusters than with the shapes of halos. This is consistent with the predictions of general relativity.

Soft-mechanical materials with memory exhibit complex mechanical properties influenced by their composition, structure, and environmental conditions. In contrast, soft-deformable particle systems, comprising numerous particles with weak interactions, have been found to behave like liquids. However, our research reveals that a specific type of soft-deformable particle system, consisting of flexible fibers with weak interactions, can develop long-term memory of applied strains even when it behaves like a liquid. This property is characterized by non-linear stress-strain relationships and a non-elastic component that increases with strain amplitude. Furthermore, our findings show that this memory effect is highly dependent on the persistence length of the fibers and the strength of the fiber-fiber interactions.

The melting behavior of gold nanoparticles with diameters ranging from 2 to 5 nanometers was examined using molecular dynamics simulations. These simulations revealed that smaller gold nanoparticles are more thermodynamically stable and exhibit higher melting points than their bulk counterparts. As the nanoparticles transition from the solid to the liquid phase, their structural organization undergoes a significant transformation. Specifically, at the onset of melting, the core of the nanoparticle begins to adopt a liquid state while the surface remains crystalline, with the formation of distinct solid-liquid interfaces. This phenomenon is characterized by the emergence of surface melting in nanoparticles, a concept distinct from the traditional bulk phenomenon.

The work examines a quasi-linear elliptic boundary value problem where the dependent variable's derivatives are discontinuous, with the discontinuity occurring across surfaces within the domain. By relaxing standard assumptions on smoothness, it is possible to analyze a broader range of problems. The solution process involves two main steps: first, a linear elliptic equation is solved to establish a reference solution, and second, the difference between this reference solution and the original solution is analyzed. This approach is used to establish the existence of weak solutions for the original problem and is applied to a specific example involving a composite material with a sharp interface.

We've developed a comprehensive model incorporating a horizontal gauge symmetry, specifically $SU(2)_H$, to address both horizontal and flavor $U(1)_A$ anomalies. This model introduces a new quark-lepton vector doublet and a new scalar doublet, enabling the spontaneous breaking of $SU(2)_H$ and $U(1)_A$ symmetries, as well as generating a $Z'_2$ symmetry for the new quark-lepton fields. As a result, one of the quarks is confined, while the other becomes a leptophilic fermion. This setup naturally resolves both anomalies and results in a unique mass pattern for the quark-lepton fields, leading to distinct phenomenological implications.

This paper derives identities for the $(h;q)$-Genocchi numbers and polynomials by utilizing the fermionic p-adic q-integral on Zp and the Frobenius-Genocchi polynomials associated with the p-adic logarithm.

This study focuses on the average reward reinforcement learning problem in non-stationary environments. A new approach is proposed, which combines a previously established lower bound for non-stationary settings and a modified version of the existing learning algorithm. This modified version is designed to handle non-stationarity by utilizing a moving target. A new algorithm, the moving target Q-learning algorithm, is derived from this concept. This algorithm is proven to be optimal within a framework that accounts for both the target's speed and the existing lower bound. As a result, it achieves the optimal regret bound up to a constant factor for both the minimax and average regret settings. This result holds true for both the known and unknown transition models. Furthermore, we establish a regret bound for the minimax setting in the case of known transition models. This result is validated through numerical experiments.

The causal odds ratio is a measure of the causal impact of a treatment on an outcome and can be estimated from observational data using a specific model that takes into account confounders. This work develops a new method for estimating this ratio based on the risk difference formula and the inverse probability of treatment weighting technique. This method is tested under various conditions and is found to be reliable in both simulated and real-world data sets. Additionally, the method is used to analyze the relationship between breast cancer treatment and long-term survival.

A novel approach to constructing autoencoders utilizing invertible layers has been developed, which employs a unique, non-differentiable, and probabilistic loss function. This method leverages the ability of invertible layers to yield Gaussian outputs, facilitating the implementation of a log-likelihood objective. Experimental findings indicate that this construction yields superior results, with notable improvements in log-likelihood and sample quality. Furthermore, the invertible autoencoder exhibits enhanced robustness to various perturbations, including those introduced by adversarial attacks.

This paper presents a visualization framework that facilitates the exploration of large-scale smart city datasets. The framework's architecture is rooted in the analysis workflow, which is further segmented into various data stages. We have developed a range of visualizations and visualization strategies tailored to showcase the progression of data at each stage. These visualizations are designed to empower researchers, developers, and stakeholders to effectively comprehend and communicate the insights derived from smart city data analysis.

In the context of hybridizable discontinuous Galerer-Keller methods, the linear systems resulting from the pre-conditioned Navier-Stokes equations can be efficiently solved using geometric multigrid preconditioners. These methods exhibit optimal geometric multigrid properties, meaning that the number of multigrid iterations remains constant with respect to the system's size, even when the coarsest grid is significantly coarser than the original discretization. This property is crucial for achieving high-performance solutions in large-scale simulations. This work presents a comprehensive study on the optimal geometric multigrid properties of HDG methods, focusing on the pre-conditioned Navier-Stokes equations. We analyze the convergence of multigrid methods for various types of discretizations, including the gradient-Laplacian and non-gradient-Laplacian formulations. Our results demonstrate that the multigrid methods exhibit optimal performance in both two and three dimensions, even when the coarsest grid is significantly coarser than the original discretization. This work provides a theoretical foundation for the optimal geometric multigrid properties of HDG methods, which is essential for achieving high-performance solutions in large-scale simulations.

The E-value serves as a probability-based measure for evaluating evidence, its
strength and reliability. In Bayesian networks, the E-value quantifies the
probability of an unobserved variable matching its inferred distribution, given
observed data. This E-value- based approach has been used to establish robust
causal conclusions from incomplete datasets, by considering all possible
combinations of missing data. However, the existing E-value lacks a clear
interpretation as a probability, and its application with multiple missing
data patterns remains unexplored. This study addresses these limitations by
introducing a novel E-value, which is grounded in the conditional probability
of a hypothesis given the observed data. This new E-value is then utilized to
assess the robustness of causal conclusions from incomplete datasets, and its
application is demonstrated through a case study involving a real-world survey.

Crossover trials are a widely used research design in which each participant receives multiple doses of an experimental treatment in sequential order. This design has several benefits, including reduced sample size and shorter study duration, but it also poses significant challenges, particularly when dealing with missing data. In crossover studies, the issue of missing data is particularly problematic due to the limited number of participants and the resulting large number of unit withdrawal rates. Our research focuses on developing a new statistical method to analyze crossover trials with missing data, which involves a two-stage process. First, we use a Bayesian model to estimate the missing data, and then we use a hierarchical model to estimate the treatment effect. This approach is particularly useful when the missing data mechanism is not fully understood, and we can only make assumptions about the underlying effect. Our method is applied to a real-world study examining the safety and efficacy of a new treatment for infantile hemangioma, and we compare its results to those obtained from a complete-case analysis and a method that imputes missing data.

The geometric interpretation of a category's nerve relates to A_n structures, specifically displaying an A_3 characteristic. This is analogous to how topological spaces are characterized by a certain quotient map exhibiting Q_2 structure in the work of Quillen.

A novel DRAM Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) is proposed that leverages the inherent properties of DRAM to provide robust and high-throughput solutions for secure applications. By exploiting the memory bias characteristics of DRAM, the new PUF can generate unique identifiers that are resilient to various forms of manipulation and attacks. Performance evaluation of the new PUF reveals that it surpasses existing solutions in both robustness and efficiency, with a success rate of over 99.9% and a throughput of more than 100,000 identifiers per second.

Network virtualization has led to the creation of Virtual Network (V) elements that are managed by V-orchestration systems. These V-orchestration systems manage V elements by executing specific actions. In this study, we introduce a functional programming approach to manage virtualized network resources. Our design transforms network orchestration actions into pure functions, separating them from their dual effects on network state. This separation allows for the management of network states through pure functions, enabling the creation of complex network configurations through functional composition. We also introduce a Network State Monad (NSM) to facilitate the management of network states in a modular and composable way. Our approach is demonstrated by applying the NSM to manage V-orchestration actions and network states in an OpenStack-based network environment.

To assess the accuracy of quantum gate operations, benchmarking protocols are utilized, which are crucial for evaluating the efficacy of quantum hardware. We introduce a novel quantum benchmarking protocol, which is based on the quantum circuit architecture of the toric code and can be implemented on any quantum hardware platform. This protocol is designed to be fault-tolerant and can be used to assess the performance of quantum gates in the presence of errors. We also present a method to efficiently extract relevant information from the output of the protocol, making it suitable for large-scale quantum simulations. Furthermore, we discuss the connection between our protocol and existing quantum benchmarks, as well as its potential for implementation on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices.

We introduce Universal Worker System (UWS), a novel approach to job execution in computing clusters, which treats jobs as worker requests and leverages a shared stateful worker pool. UWS enables workers to be dynamically assigned, reassigned, or removed on-demand, facilitating job reuse through partial computation caching. Our evaluation of UWS on a 512-core supercomputer demonstrates its benefits in performance, energy efficiency, and resource occupancy, which can also extend to large-scale high-performance computing clusters.

The emergence of wireless communications and networking technologies is transforming the way we live and work, with the 5G system already being used in various applications and the sixth generation network being developed. Despite significant advancements, there is still a lack of understanding about the underlying technologies, particularly among those outside the industry. This article aims to bridge that knowledge gap by providing an accessible overview of wireless communications and networking systems, specifically tailored for students. A unique approach is taken to introduce these systems through blockchain-based learning, where a blockchain network is used to support a decentralized education system. This framework is designed to be user-friendly, with the goal of making complex concepts more approachable. A comprehensive analysis of the proposed system is conducted, with a focus on its technical feasibility and limitations. This innovative approach has the potential to revolutionize the way we learn about wireless communications and networking technologies, and we believe it can also be applied to other complex fields.

The James Webb Space Telescope is set to capture the first-ever spectra of Earth-like exoplanets, revealing their atmospheric composition. However, the exact wavelengths for this analysis are still uncertain. To address this, we simulated the atmospheres of terrestrial exoplanets, assuming a simplified composition of CO2, H2O, O2, and CH4. Our results indicate that the strongest signals appear in the 0.6-5.0 micrometer range. We also found that the ratio of O2 to CO2 can be used to infer the presence of liquid water, while the presence of O2 is affected by the host star's temperature. Additionally, we discovered that the presence of H2O and O3 can be used to infer the presence of liquid water and atmospheric temperature, respectively. Our findings suggest that the 3-5.5 micrometer range is the most suitable for analyzing the atmospheres of Earth-like exoplanets, while the 3.1-3.5 micrometer range is the most suitable for analyzing the presence of liquid water.

We have developed a theoretical framework to study the behavior of surface currents in both bosonic and fermionic systems, based on the concept of "chiral quantum dynamics." Our research reveals that these surface currents exhibit a high degree of robustness across different systems, including non-interacting fermions, the Bose-Hubbard model, and chiral topological insulators. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the total surface current in a given region remains consistent across different parts of the system, as long as the local density does not change sign. Additionally, our study provides a mathematical proof for the total surface current in a region with uniform density.

Our research focuses on developing a multilingual neural machine translation model capable of translating into multiple languages from a single source. We've successfully adapted a model to translate medical texts from a single source language into various targets while leveraging a vast medical translation corpus. The adapted model outperforms a baseline model lacking domain-specific adaptation on an out-of-domain medical text test set. Additionally, we've discovered that incorporating specific medical subdomains during training enhances the model's performance.

This research delves into the theoretical analysis of the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation's potential in modeling the behavior of dusty plasma waves. The study focuses on how ion fluid temperature and electron nonthermal behavior influence the formation of solitary and shock waves in dusty plasmas. The results show that within a specific range of parameters, shock waves can form, whereas outside this range, solitary waves can develop. The study also reveals that the ion fluid temperature and electron nonthermal behavior have a significant impact on the formation of shock waves. The findings suggest that the non-Gaussian velocity distribution function can lead to the formation of shock waves in dusty plasmas. The study's results could provide valuable insights for future space missions, particularly those exploring the lower atmosphere of the sun.

Contrastive learning has become a crucial aspect of unsupervised representation learning. It's been shown that contrastive tasks can be more effective at learning representations than the standard pre-training task of masked language modeling. However, the scarcity of contrastive tasks for pre-training in multilingual settings has hindered its adoption. We introduce a novel task, contrastive context prediction, which involves predicting a sentence's context without using the sentence itself. This task is more effective in low-resource languages and allows for more informative context representations. We also propose a novel contrastive loss, called CCP loss, which outperforms the standard contrastive loss. Our experiments show that this new task and loss significantly improve sentence representations in low-resource languages and achieve state-of-the-art results on various cross-lingual tasks.

In this research, we introduce a straightforward yet powerful technique to enhance multimodal learning, specifically designed for scenarios where one modality develops its representation more slowly than others. Our method, called Prototypical Modality Rebalance (PMR), is based on the idea that the slower modality's representation benefits from being compared to faster modalities. We achieve this by integrating a contrastive loss into the slower modality's loss function. Our experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that PMR can effectively bridge the gap between slow and fast modalities, leading to improved performance.

We derive kinetic equations for massless fermions in a spacetime environment with non-zero local particle number density divergence. Our results are compared to the established kinetic equations for neutral and charged fermions in a flat spacetime with uniform currents, and we also consider the applicability to the quark-antiquark system in a quark-gluon plasma.

This study presents a CNN+(TT-DNN) model that leverages a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract key features and a two-stage time-depth neural network (TT-DNN) to enhance command recognition accuracy. The TT-DNN model is comprised of two stages: a TT-DNN that extracts features from a pre-trained CNN and a TT-DNN that combines these features to generate a final command recognition decision. The TT-DNN is trained using a two-stage approach, with the first stage utilizing randomly initialized weights and the second stage utilizing the pre-trained weights from the initial stage. The model is trained using the Google Speech Command Dataset and achieves an accuracy of 96.5% on the English command recognition benchmark, surpassing the accuracy of a traditional CNN model by 1.5%.

We investigate the behavior of a quantum system initially placed in a specific energy state, under the influence of an external driving force that interacts with a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. This interaction leads to a complex time-evolution governed by a Schrödinger equation, where the Hamiltonian is replaced by a matrix that combines real and imaginary components. By analyzing the long-term behavior of this system, we find that its evolution is determined by the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian, which can be either real or complex conjugates. When the eigenvalues are real, the system exhibits a periodic pattern, whereas when they are complex conjugates, the system's behavior is described by the principles of quantum mechanics. Our results are further supported by numerical simulations that demonstrate the feasibility of our approach.

We have developed a method to enhance the efficiency of plasmonic solar cells by optimizing the design of their nanoantenna structures. This approach utilizes a genetic algorithm to maximize energy conversion efficiency, taking into account the specific wavelength and intensity of incident light. As an example, we analyzed a plasmonic system consisting of aluminum nanoparticles and light with a Gaussian distribution between 400-900 nm and an intensity of 1.5 suns. Under these conditions, we found that aluminum nanoparticles with a specific design achieved a maximum conversion efficiency of 75.4%, significantly surpassing the efficiency of traditional solar cells.

We introduce a novel approach to modeling computational processes by combining an algebraic framework for binary relations with a linear-time modal logic. This hybrid methodology leverages the linear-time logic's capacity for temporal reasoning with the algebraic framework's ability to capture various sequential and simultaneous process combinations. The resulting hybrid structure is then utilized to establish a comprehensive framework for categorizing the computational processes' expressive power. This framework is based on the inherent properties of the processes, such as continuity, decidability, and the ability to be expressed in finite forms. The established framework is then applied to a diverse range of finite and infinite computational processes, including pushdown systems, Petri nets, counter systems, and linear-time automata.

Deep neural networks have been increasingly applied to image processing tasks, such as denoising and compression, in recent years. However, the limited processing capabilities of current hardware systems hinder the full potential of these networks. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed, integrating a frequency-domain hardware architecture with a low-latency, model-free processing engine. This allows for the efficient implementation of complex neural network models, including the FDHT-LSTM, which outperforms traditional model-based hardware designs in terms of speed and power efficiency. As a result, the FDHT-LSTM model achieves a significant improvement in processing speed, with a 2.5 times increase in throughput, and a 1.5 times reduction in energy consumption, compared to state-of-the-art model-based hardware designs.

This research investigates the security of MAVLink protocol, a standard communication standard among unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). The study reveals that the current protocol lacks robust security features, rendering it vulnerable to various attacks. To address this, MAVLink message encryption is explored, and several symmetric and asymmetric encryption algorithms are tested for efficiency. The results show that AES-128 encryption offers the most efficient data transmission for MAVLink messages. Additionally, a cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the GStreamer video processing framework is identified, and its impact on MAVLink protocol security is discussed.

Network emulation is a crucial tool for studying how networks function. Developing an accurate emulation environment that replicates real-world network behavior is a significant challenge. This paper presents a novel approach to network emulation that leverages the concept of end-to-end properties, which are fundamental characteristics of networks. By using this approach, a simpler network model can be created, as it focuses on the interactions between end-to-end nodes, rather than the intricate network infrastructure. This enables the separation of network behavior from the specifics of network technology, making it a more versatile tool for analysis. This paper outlines the theoretical framework for this approach, illustrates its application in various network scenarios, and discusses its practical implications.

A novel, twistorial approach to the Newman-Penrose (N-P) map is presented, which offers a geometrically invariant formulation. This new formulation is derived from the N-P map's original representation using the spinor zilberberg twist, which transforms the original N-P equations into twistorial form. This reformulation is then applied to the Kerr-Newman spacetime, yielding a set of twistorial equations that define the spacetime's geometric properties.

The Muon-Specimen telescope is a novel, large-scale, and non-invasive device for analyzing archaeological sites, capable of detecting objects as small as 3 meters in depth. This cutting-edge technology employs a cosmic ray muon detector to create detailed 2D images of buried relics. This innovative system boasts a wide range of potential applications, including the detection of historical artifacts in archaeological sites, monitoring cultural heritage sites, and analyzing the structural integrity of buildings. This paper outlines the Muon-Specimen telescope's design, implementation, and initial findings, as well as its potential applications and future development prospects.

A novel algorithm for Probabilistic Edge-Grammar Linearized Lattices has been developed, which is an extension of GLL parsing. This new approach, PEGLL, offers enhanced flexibility by supporting arbitrary grammars, as opposed to context-free structures exclusive to GLL. Additionally, PEGLL provides a means of integrating pre-existing LLLs generated from distinct grammars, thereby facilitating the creation of customized LLLs.

The process of thermal radiation in a single-mode cavity, occurring between two levels of arbitrary energy, is examined. It's demonstrated that this process becomes kinematically viable at infinite temperatures, yet the radiation rate remains zero. This result stems from the fact that thermal averages of initial and final states become indistinguishable. A similar scenario applies to stimulated emission in a two-level system, where infinite temperatures are reached due to simultaneous occupancy of both ground and excited states.

To better comprehend how humans respond to surprising language, researchers have been studying the relationship between predictability and surprise. However, current research has primarily focused on individual words within a limited context, which may not accurately capture the full range of language predictability. In this study, we introduce a new approach to predictability that takes into account much longer contexts, using a neural network model to predict words across multiple sentences. Our results show that this new method is effective at predicting human language preferences, and can also be used to identify previously known and newly discovered language patterns. Furthermore, we find that incorporating longer contexts reveals new insights into how people process language, and that this new approach can be applied to other areas of study, such as understanding how people process language to answer questions.

In this research, we introduce a novel approach to 3D object estimation that leverages a multi-stage training scheme. Our method trains the network to learn a set of standard poses for each class individually, thereby enhancing the overall generalization capability of the model. We achieve this by implementing a self-supervised scheme that generates a diverse set of pseudo-perspective views for each class, making it easier for the network to learn a comprehensive set of standard poses. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach significantly improves the performance of 3D object estimation models, particularly when combined with a rotationally invariant module. Our code is publicly available for download.

We investigate the influence of intrinsic spin-orbit coupling on the behavior of InSb nanowire quantum dots, taking into account the effects of both single and double electron occupancy. Our research reveals that the application of a magnetic field at the C point leads to the formation of distinct, non-interacting electron and hole states, which are separated by a finite energy gap. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the presence of this magnetic field significantly enhances the coupling between the electron and hole states, resulting in a substantial increase in the hybridization energy. Our findings suggest that the properties of InSb nanowire quantum dots make them an attractive candidate for the study of spin qubits, particularly when combined with a strong magnetic field.

The traditional approach to modeling particle dynamics in the solar wind involves using simplified 2D models, which assume particles follow a fixed trajectory. However, this assumption is challenged by the complex and dynamic nature of the solar wind's magnetic field. To address this limitation, we've developed a 3D model that incorporates the effects of pitch-angle scattering. Our results show that this modification significantly alters the energy distribution of particles, particularly in regions with closed magnetic field lines. Furthermore, we've found that the 2D model underestimates the energy distribution of protons in the solar wind by a factor of 2.5. To validate our findings, we've analyzed in situ measurements from the Parker Solar Probe and discovered a striking agreement between the 3D model and the data.

The recent measurement of the Higgs diphoton decay rate by the CMS collaboration is significantly higher than the standard model prediction, prompting an investigation into the possibility of extended scalar sectors that could enhance the Higgs diphoton signal. This study examines the impact of such sectors on the Higgsstrahlung process, which is a key process for testing the Higgs potential and can be measured through the di-Higgs invariant mass distribution. By analyzing the relationship between the Higgs diphoton and di-Higgs processes, we demonstrate that certain scenarios that increase the Higgs diphoton signal do not necessarily enhance the Higgsstrahlung signal. Furthermore, we find that the Higgsstrahlung process can even be reduced in certain cases, which would require a reduction in the Higgs diphoton signal.

The joint numerical radius of a tuple of linear operators on a finite dimensional complex space serves as a useful tool for analyzing various properties of these operators. Key properties and applications of the joint numerical radius are explored, including its role in best approximation problems and the numerical range of operator products.

This study explores the application of DP-SGD and PATE frameworks to ensure privacy in financial predictive models, comparing their performance in both regression and classification tasks. We assess the trade-offs between these frameworks' performance, robustness, and computational overhead in financial risk management scenarios. Our analysis reveals that PATE outperforms DP-SGD in terms of both privacy and accuracy, with PATE also exhibiting greater stability and computational efficiency. However, DP-SGD offers a more adaptable approach to balancing privacy and accuracy, with its flexibility in trade-off settings allowing for greater flexibility in achieving desired levels of both.

The general Wold type decomposition is extended to multivariate second-order random distribution fields. Conditions for the uncorrelated innovations in the general Wold type decomposition are established. Additionally, a specific Wold type decomposition is also established for multivariate random fields.

This study investigates the influence of a laser on a gas mixture containing dust or impurities.  The gas mixture is modeled using the Drude model for dielectric materials, while the dust or impurities are represented by a two-temperature non-conductive material.  The one-dimensional Boltzmann equation and Maxwell's equations are used to simulate the system.  The results show that the presence of dust or impurities can alter the system's ignition characteristics, potentially leading to detonation under specific conditions.

This study presents a new boundary-aware segmentation network, dubbed BASNet, which effectively isolates target objects within images. BASNet's core feature is its ability to identify boundaries between the target object and its surroundings, allowing it to focus on the object's interior. This approach is made possible by a novel decoder and a boundary-aware loss function. The BASNet architecture is flexible, allowing it to be paired with a range of decoders, and it achieves state-of-the-art results in various segmentation tasks. Furthermore, BASNet exhibits strong generalizability and performs well in real-world applications, such as medical imaging and image segmentation in complex environments.

This paper introduces the Driver Messenger System (DMS) that enables vehicles to safely change lanes by sending signals to drivers of adjacent vehicles, rather than broadcasting to all vehicles on the scene. The DMS system consists of a sender vehicle, a receiver vehicle, and an adjacent vehicle in the target lane, to alert the receiver's driver of an available lane. The paper examines the effectiveness of DMS in enhancing lane change safety through a comparative study with other cooperative lane change methods. Furthermore, it investigates the optimal receiver vehicle placement to minimize the risk of collision.

Active particles known as run-and-tumble particles in a two-dimensional environment have been studied extensively. These particles, modeled as two-dimensional versions of a specific type of particle motion, have been shown to exhibit a range of behaviors when interacting with different boundaries. In this work, we develop a theoretical framework to understand the movement of these active particles near various boundaries, including reflective surfaces, channels, and specific types of boundaries. By applying this framework, we derive several key results, including the calculation of particle currents, the determination of particle trajectories, and the characterization of particle behavior near specific boundaries, such as the analysis of particle currents and the determination of particle currents.

The electronic structure calculations for atomic states in plasmas are typically based on the average atom model, which uses a multigroup approach to describe the energy levels. However, this method can be computationally expensive due to the need to solve large systems of equations for each energy group. To improve this, a new average atom model has been developed that utilizes Siegert states, which are a more detailed representation of atomic states, to reduce computational costs. The new model has been implemented and tested in a specific context, namely the high-temperature water steam environment of a pressurized water reactor, and has been shown to provide more accurate results at lower computational costs.

We have conducted a detailed investigation of the plasma dynamics in a solar flare event, specifically focusing on the plasma flows in the active region NOAA 12673. Our analysis of the Si IV 1394.8 and 1402.8 Angstroms spectra from the SLIT, a spectrometer, revealed a redshifted component in the Si IV line, which we believe is caused by a secondary component in the plasma flows. We have developed a model to explain the observed effect, which takes into account the Doppler shift and the effect of the plasma's velocity gradient. Our model is consistent with the observed effect, and we have found that the velocity of the plasma flows is approximately 100-200 km/s. We have also found that the observed effect is consistent with the expected value of the Doppler shift, and that the velocity of the plasma flows is approximately 100-200 km/s. Our analysis suggests that the observed effect is a result of the plasma flows in the active region, which is consistent with the expected dynamics of the solar flare event.

In the context of quantum chromodynamics, the solution to the strong CP problem is obtained when theta is greater than zero, requiring the breaking of Baryon and Baryon-Lepton symmetries to be sufficiently large. To investigate this, we calculate the neutron and delta electric dipole moments using chiral perturbation theory at the next-to-leading order, finding that the neutron and delta EDMs are directly proportional to theta and can be expressed as delta and delta_n respectively. Additionally, the ratio of the neutron and delta EDMs is found to be approximately 0.56, which is consistent with recent experimental findings.

The topological changes in thin films due to ion irradiation are investigated through a geometric lens, focusing on the interface's behavior within a two-dimensional amorphous structure. The study employs a random packing model to represent the initial disordered state of the film. Following irradiation, the formation of topological defects and the subsequent relaxation process are analyzed through a sequence of geometric operations, including the introduction of pairs of defects and the subsequent rearrangement of the interface. These operations reveal a relationship between the number of defects and the length of the interface, as well as the rate at which the interface moves. The study's findings are compared to experimental results and the underlying assumptions are discussed.

The Router concept transforms source code into a unique, paraphrased form, making it difficult to recognize as original: it maintains the code's functionality while altering its wording. By doing so, the code loses its identical copy status, thus evading plagiarism detection. This paper outlines a method for creating paraphrased code that preserves its functionality by generating paraphrased equivalent statements. The approach utilizes a combination of two distinct sequence-to-sequence neural networks, each trained on a different dataset. The first network, utilizing a standard corpus of paraphrased sentences, generates paraphrased input statements, while the second network, trained on a paraphrased code corpus, produces paraphrased output statements. The two networks are combined to generate paraphrased code. The proposed approach was tested using a dataset of 1,500 C++ functions, with the results demonstrating that the generated paraphrased code maintains its original functionality.

We investigate Dirichlet series in the class $\mathcal{M}_\varepsilon$ and demonstrate a minimum value for their abscissa of absolute convergence, $\sigma_a$, is $\varepsilon + 1/2$. This conclusion is drawn from the development of a specific type of Dirichlet polynomial known as a Riemann zeta-like function, which is defined as $F_s(n) = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{1}{j^1-\varepsilon + \frac{\gamma}{2}} \cos(\log j\sqrt{s})$.

This research explores the properties of approximate subgroup structures on finite groups with specific characteristics.  We demonstrate that for finite groups with bounded exponent, approximately embedded $(k,r)$-metric subgroups exhibit a uniform polynomial structure, and a finite collection of such structures can be combined to form a larger, well-defined $(k,r)$-metric approximate subgroup.  Additionally, we establish that for finite groups with bounded exponent, approximately embedded $(k,r)$-metric approximate subgroups can be decomposed into a finite union of normal, well-defined $(k,r)$-metric approximate subgroups.

We introduce novel algorithms based on randomized and Nesterov smoothing, tailored to log-concave maximum likelihood estimation. These algorithms utilize importance sampling and a Nesterov acceleration technique, respectively. Notably, they offer the first acceleration of log-concave empirical risk minimization when using sampling weights. Moreover, they demonstrate global convergence under mild conditions, ensuring a positive lower bound for the log-concave function. Experimental results on image deblurring and text classification demonstrate the efficacy of these algorithms.

This article introduces the 'Visit All Or Lose' game, where two players compete to see who can access the most vertices of a connected graph. The game's rules are straightforward: players take turns selecting a vertex to visit, and no vertex can be visited more than once. The player with the most visited vertices at the end of the game wins. Our analysis reveals that the number of vertices an optimal player can visit is at most $2n-2$, where $n$ is the number of vertices in the graph. Notably, this upper limit is achievable in certain special cases, such as for specific types of graphs. The game's upper limit is equivalent to the chromatic toughness of the graph minus one. The spectral density of a stochastic process encapsulates its frequency-dependent patterns, offering a distinctive representation of the underlying random motion. This paper explores the spectral density of continuous time random walks (CTRWs) and establishes a method to differentiate between distinct stochastic processes through the spectral density function. By considering CTRW models with varying waiting time and jump distributions, we derive the spectral density, which can be experimentally measured and analyzed to distinguish between different stochastic processes driving a given behavior.
This research paper demonstrates the solvability of the higher-order Broer-Kaup system through the application of Riemann-type reduction symmetries and symbolic computation.

A unique combination of vorticity and a density gradient in nonuniform flow results in an energy source that can be balanced by a specific interaction term. This interaction term is influenced by the gradient of vorticity and the product of fluid density and its velocity. This paper aims to derive this balance from fundamental principles and derive the corresponding equation. Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that the derived equation aligns with the Euler equation when vorticity is zero, leading to energy conservation. Additionally, it will be shown that the interaction term is zero when density is uniform, resulting in the conservation of total energy.

VIRUP is a visualization tool for particle-based simulations that is written in C++ and utilizes OpenGL. This paper introduces a Python binding and scripting interface for VIRUP, enabling users to streamline their workflow and automate tasks like scene selection, camera positioning, and rendering of image sequences. This scripting interface is particularly beneficial for researchers who need to create custom visualizations or work with large datasets, and for researchers who prefer to work in an interactive, iterative manner.

This paper outlines the conceptual framework and initial findings of the Data Bricks Space Mission, a space-themed outreach initiative aimed at educating the public about data and AI concepts. This school-led project targets students aged 11-18 and operates within the UK, providing a unique, teacher-driven experience that fosters a data-driven understanding of the universe.

In Software-Defined Networking (SDN), data-path verification is a critical task, 
as it ensures that the actual data paths created by SDN controllers match the 
expected ones. To verify data paths, a controller uses openflow describe and 
describe flow delete commands to query the data path created in the switches. 
However, these commands can cause a significant load on switches and the data 
plane due to the frequent iteration over flow entries, resulting in a substantial 
network traffic generation. This issue is addressed by the OpenFlow design team 
by introducing the Flow Watcher concept, which enables the reduction of this 
iteration. Our research presents a novel approach to minimize the iteration over 
flow entries, resulting in a significant reduction in network traffic and a 
substantial reduction in the number of data plane operations.

A common issue with generative models is that adjusting their latent space attributes often results in unwanted changes to the generated image. To overcome this, we propose a novel approach to adjust generated images by manipulating their latent codes. Our method, which we call disentangled style adjustment, relies on the assumption that the latent code is weakly separated from the image generation process. This separation enables us to make targeted adjustments to the style of generated images without disrupting their overall representation. Our approach leverages the style transfer capabilities of adversarial style interpolation networks, which we demonstrate using a single image using a pre-trained StyleGAN model. Our results show that this method can produce high-quality style-interpolated images that are both aesthetically pleasing and semantically consistent.

This study investigates the aerodynamic interactions between two identical two-foil structures, with a focus on one foil's performance. The investigation is conducted using a combination of experimental and computational methods, with a particular emphasis on determining the optimal gap size between the foils. The research reveals that the gap size significantly affects the performance of the trailing foil, with a narrow gap resulting in increased lift and a wider gap resulting in increased drag. A specific gap size is identified as the optimal configuration, leading to a balance between increased lift and drag. The study also examines the complex wake patterns behind the foils, including the presence of a recirculating bubble behind the leading foil, which is found to be influenced by the gap size. The research provides a detailed analysis of the flow structures behind the foils, including the presence of a leading edge vortex and a trailing edge vortex, which are found to be responsible for the lift and drag coefficients of the trailing foil. The study also investigates the effect of the gap size on the wake velocity deficit, which is found to be influenced by the gap size and the aspect ratio of the foil.

In the study of quantum field theories, spectral functions are often used as a crucial tool for analyzing time-dependent processes. Unfortunately, extracting these functions from real-time data is an ill-defined problem, which has led to the use of alternative methods such as fitting to a few correlation functions. Our research shows that these approaches are flawed, as they neglect the complex correlations that are necessary for accurate spectral reconstruction. To address this issue, we have developed a novel method that involves using a neural network to learn a non-linear mapping between correlation functions and spectral functions. Our results demonstrate that this method can achieve accurate results even when only a limited amount of data is available, and it can also be used to identify the optimal parameters of the spectral function. Furthermore, we have shown that our method can be applied to a wide range of theories, including those with different numbers of particles and different types of interactions.

We suggest employing a quantum dot as a highly sensitive tool to investigate the addition spectrum of a superconductor. The quantum dot, which is in contact with the superconductor, is comprised of a double quantum well structure, and its electronic state can be manipulated by adjusting the distance between its wells. When the quantum dot is connected to a normal lead through a tunneling barrier, it can be used to probe the superconductor's addition spectrum. The resulting current flowing through the quantum dot can be measured as a function of the applied gate voltage, which determines the energy level of the quantum dot. Our research demonstrates that the quantum dot can be effectively utilized to identify the energy of the quasiparticles within the superconductor's energy gap.

The creation of new drug molecules is a crucial aspect of drug development, which has seen significant advancements with the aid of generative models. However, the current methods primarily focus on generating molecules that closely resemble existing ones, limiting their ability to create novel molecules. This paper introduces a generative model that leverages a graph attention network to create new drug molecules by learning from their relationships. By employing a graph attention network, the model effectively captures the complex interactions between the drug molecule's components. We evaluate the model's performance on two datasets and compare it to existing state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating its ability to generate novel and diverse drug molecules. Furthermore, the model's capacity to generate molecules with specific properties is also explored.

This study introduces the Dynamic GoI Machine (DGoIM), a new abstract machine within the Intensional Logic of Partial Maps framework, which has been previously established as a computational model. By examining the underlying principles of DGoIM, we can categorize it as a sequential abstract machine, characterized by a push stack, with a limited capacity for parallel processing. Furthermore, DGoIM's capabilities align with the principles of the lambda calculus within the call-by-value paradigm, with some modifications, and its operational semantics can be viewed as a form of higher-order pushdown system. Notably, DGoIM's operational behavior is found to be equivalent to that of the sequent calculus in Lambda Calculus.

The Large Magellanic Cloud is the second-largest satellite galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, and its star formation history is still not well understood. To study the galaxy's star formation, researchers have used various datasets, but these have limitations in terms of their spatial resolution and color information. To overcome these limitations, researchers have developed a machine learning model that can analyze images of the galaxy and identify its star-forming regions. The model uses a combination of photometric and spatial data to classify the galaxy's regions, and its performance is comparable to that of a human expert. The model has also been used to identify areas of the galaxy that are actively forming stars, and these regions are consistent with previous findings. The model has the potential to be used to study other galaxies and galaxies in the Milky Way's halo.

A significant concern in the field of electricity consumption is the issue of theft, necessitating the development of an efficient detection system. This study introduces a novel, time-series based approach to identify potential electricity thieves, leveraging the inherent temporal patterns in consumption data. Our proposed model outperforms existing methods by incorporating temporal features and adaptability, as evidenced by its superior performance on the ULA1 dataset.

In a previous study, we established a categorization system for surface graphs based on their base graphs. Utilizing this framework, we have identified the irreducible base graphs for the torus and sphere, revealing 9 and 11 unique base graphs respectively. Our research has also involved determining the sparsest and tight surface graphs by combining these irreducible bases in various configurations.

Our research marks the first time the lifetime of the $\Omega^0_c$ baryon has been measured in the decay into $\rm K^{-} \pi^{+} \pi^{-} n$.  Using a dataset of 1.3 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collisions captured by the LHCb detector at 7 TeV centre-of-mass energy, we identified $\Omega^0_c$ baryons decaying into the specified final state and determined their lifetimes to be 148.7 $\pm$ 5.1 fs with statistical and systematic uncertainties of 2.0, 1.2, and 1.1 fs respectively.  This result is consistent with previous findings but surpasses their precision, and it also surpasses the world's most precise measurement which had an uncertainty of 14%.

A novel approach to clustering sparse subspace clustering (SSC) is presented, which leverages the sparsity of the subspace signal in a tree-structured basis. This method, called sparse tree clustering (STC), utilizes a hierarchical algorithm to identify clusters at varying scales. STC is more efficient than traditional SSC methods, utilizing the spatial structure of the data to reduce computational complexity while improving performance. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of STC, which is implemented in a Python package available at https://github.com/Chen-Rui/STC.

The formation of melt ponds on Arctic sea ice has a significant impact on the sea ice's energy balance, affecting its albedo and consequently the rate of melt. However, the current models of melt ponds are limited by their reliance on empirical assumptions and their inability to account for the complex processes involved in melt pond formation. In this study, a new melt pond model is developed that incorporates the fundamental principles of melt pond growth and the physical processes driving it. The model is based on a one-dimensional framework that incorporates the principles of energy balance, the transport of heat and salt, and the dynamics of melt pond formation and decay. The model is validated using data from the Arctic Transpolar Shipborne Experiment and is shown to accurately simulate the observed melt pond coverage and the seasonal melt pond evolution from satellite imagery.

We've developed a theoretical model explaining the atom-molecule scattering process in the ground state of 39K84Rb, which is based on the spin-orbit model. The model's parameters are determined by experimental data on the scattering cross-section and the branching ratio of the loss feature. The model's predictions accurately match the experimental data for various final spin states and molecular energies. Additionally, we found that the branching ratio is influenced by the final spin state, and we can control this by adjusting the magnetic field, such that the transition to a specific spin state can be suppressed while another spin state is enhanced.

A broad category of stochastic processes exhibiting anomalous diffusion characteristics can be described through the lens of $q$-Gaussian distributions, which are linked to correlations within these systems. These distributions naturally emerge in the context of continuous-time random walks, a model for anomalous diffusion. This study explores the relationship between the $q$-entropy and the $q$-Gaussian distribution, revealing that they are interconnected through a simple, linear transformation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the $q$-entropy is a natural consequence of the master equation governing the system, leading to the emergence of the $q$-entropy production. This relationship enables us to derive a $q$-Boltzmann-Gibbs equation and to establish a $q$-Kramers-Moyal expansion.

We explore the electronic properties of a HONLS, specifically the Tl$_3$S$_2$Pt, structure. By applying an external electric field, we can adjust the interlayer distance and alter the band structure, thereby controlling the Weyl nodes and surface Fermi arcs. Additionally, the introduction of an electric field enables the creation of a tunable topological charge tensor in the HONLS, allowing for a switch between different topological phases. Our research also reveals that the HONLS exhibits a unique property, the higher-order surface Hall effect, which can be observed in the surface states of Tl$_3$S$_2$Pt.

Decentralized computing systems often face the challenge of managing resources from unverified nodes, which can compromise their integrity. This study presents a reputation management protocol that utilizes a probabilistic approach to guarantee the reliability of decentralized systems. The protocol is implemented on a blockchain platform and tested using a decentralized computing environment, demonstrating the effectiveness of probabilistic reputation management in maintaining system integrity.

This study presents a novel, linear perceptual quality assessment model for point clouds. 
The model is developed by integrating a range of point-based, view-based, and hybrid distortion metrics with a deep learning approach, specifically a convolutional neural network. 
The model is trained and evaluated using data from the Virtual Reality Point Cloud (VRPC) dataset, resulting in a comprehensive evaluation of its performance and effectiveness. 
The results show that the proposed model surpasses existing objective quality metrics in predicting human subjective quality ratings, with a higher correlation coefficient and lower mean squared error.

We explore the properties of black holes in higher-dimensional spacetimes with a specific type of gravitational potential, which is analogous to a potential seen in quantum chromodynamics at high density. Our analysis shows that the black hole phase transition in the interior of spacetime corresponds to a transition in the surrounding region to a state known as quarkyonic matter, which is characterized by a specific type of confinement. We also find that the pressure in the black hole interior is related to the pressure in the quarkyonic region, which is determined by a specific type of fluid known as a stiff fluid. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the black hole phase transition is a consequence of the confinement in the quarkyonic region, which leads to a change in the pressure and a specific type of phase transition known as a first order transition.

Accurate diagnosis of knee injuries is crucial for athletes and individuals who engage in high-risk sports. Current diagnosis methods involve time-consuming and expensive magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans that require skilled interpretation.
